title: Asia’s aging population will redefine retirement, care—and independence
description: Adults in Asia are increasingly prioritizing autonomy, health, and financial security over maximizing the inheritance they leave behind.
fullText:
Over the next decade, Asian families will transfer an estimated $10 trillion—nearly twice the size of Germany's GDP—to the next generation. Yet there's a nuanced story emerging behind that headline figure. As people live longer, they're rethinking how preserve their own independence while still passing enough wealth to their children.

What percentage of assets are Asians reserving for themselves?

Why are traditional family care models under pressure?

How is longer life expectancy changing wealth transfer patterns?

What financial solutions could support independent aging strategies?

Asia is the fastest-aging region in the world. Fifteen percent of its population is over the age of 60; that share is projected to rise to 26% by 2050, according to the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific. Some of the world's longest-living populations are also in Asia, led by Hong Kong, where life expectancy is 85.5 years. In mainland China, life expectancy rose from around 52 in 1963 to 78 today.

This transformation isn't just a demographic story. Greater longevity is reshaping how people think about wealth, care, and responsibility within the family.

For generations, many in Asia assumed that wealth would be passed to children, through the funding of education and home ownership, or leaving an eventual inheritance—with children later caring for their parents in old age. But today's families are planning things differently. Our data shows that adults in Asia are increasingly prioritizing autonomy, health, and financial security over maximizing the inheritance they leave behind.

The next chapter of Asia's wealth transfer won't be defined only by the money parents leave behind. It will also be measured by something potentially more valuable: the freedom to support their own longer, more independent lives—and, in turn, relieve their children of the financial and emotional burdens of caregiving.

Manulife's Asia Care Survey 2026 of 9,000 adults across nine Asia markets, shows how far this shift towards independence has progressed. Men in Asia anticipate funding 14 years of their own care in later life, and women 15 years, at a time when fewer older people than ever are living with their adult children.

The survey's respondents overwhelmingly value independence and financial freedom over passing down tangible assets to their family. Regionwide, 83% said securing that freedom was more important than leaving their heirs the maximum amount of wealth.

Respondents plan to earmark an average of 68% of their money and assets to fund their own costs, including health care, as they age, leaving the rest to their children. This ratio varied across markets, with those in Taiwan expecting to spend the most on their own health and care at 78%, and those in the Philippines and Indonesia planning to spend the least, both at 60%.

title: Accused NC killer mom plans insanity defense — as retired judge says more may follow Lindsay Clancy strategy
description: Andrea Faust's insanity defense in her son's killing draws direct parallels to Lindsay Clancy's postpartum psychosis case as jurors deliberate.
fullText:
The insanity defense planned by a North Carolina mother accused of killing her son has drawn parallels to Lindsay Clancy's trial and raised questions about whether it could become prevalent in criminal cases.

Andrea Faust, 41, is charged with murder and attempted murder in the Feb. 12 death of her 3-year-old son and the attempted murder of her 2-year-old son at their home in Durham, North Carolina.

Her attorneys have filed notice that they intend to rely on defenses of not guilty by reason of insanity and diminished capacity, WRAL reported.

The case is drawing parallels to Clancy's Massachusetts trial. Retired Massachusetts Superior Judge Jack Lu said he expects similar defenses to be raised more often as the Clancy case draws national attention to postpartum mental-health conditions.

Lindsay Clancy Didn't Show 'Break With Reality' As Jury Weighs Psychosis Defense: Susan Smith Prosecutor

Clancy has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility in the 2023 deaths of her three children. Her defense argued she suffered from postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors argue she understood her actions and acted deliberately.

Jurors ended a second day of deliberations Friday without reaching a verdict. They will return on Monday morning to continue working toward a verdict.

In Faust's case, the filing does not establish that she was legally insane or had diminished capacity. Her attorney, Nicole Galinsky, told the local outlet that a defense expert concluded Faust could not distinguish right from wrong during the alleged murders.

"Andrea and Lindsay's cases are eerily similar, though not entirely the same," Galinsky told Fox News Digital.

Galinsky noted that Faust was not suffering from postpartum psychosis.

"However, both women were known to be loving, doting, responsible mothers who were worried about and caring for their children up until the very second they decided to kill them," Galinsky said, adding that Faust and Clancy were both struggling with similar issues, including hallucinations, hospitalizations and mental health.

"Neither woman did this out of the blue," Galinsky said in an email. "Both were struggling enormously with their mental health. But, like most women and almost all moms, they were just trying to get through each day, care for their children, be a good mom/wife/employee. Both were seeking help from doctors who weren't really taking their concerns seriously.

"Both of these cases highlight the failure in our society to take women and mothers seriously when it comes to their mental health. Both of these women advocated for themselves countless times and—for what? It got them nowhere.

"I am hopeful that our case will demonstrate how to properly treat and rehabilitate a woman living her own worst nightmare. Lindsay Clancy was not given that luxury."

Follow The Fox True Crime Team On X

Lu said society and the legal system have not fully understood the effects postpartum mental illness can have on behavior and criminal responsibility.

"Most of the time, these criminal responsibility, insanity, mental health defenses are unsuccessful," Lu told Fox News Digital.

Lindsay Clancy's Family Was 'Very Concerned' About Her Mental Health In The Months Before She Killed Her Kids

Although he is not a mental-health expert, Lu said the Clancy trial has challenged and changed his own understanding of what a person might experience.

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

"I had no real understanding of what a person like Ms. Clancy was going through until this trial," he said.

Faust was found incapable of proceeding to trial in March after court records documented serious concerns about her mental health and safety, according to WRAL.

Central Regional Hospital later found her capable of proceeding as of May 21. Her attorney said another evaluation would examine her mental state at the time of the alleged offenses.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Lu said mental-health defenses should receive more serious consideration because they can explain behavior and reduce moral culpability. But allegations involving children create an especially difficult path with jurors, he said.

"These cases should have legs," Lu said, "but unfortunately society and juries don't give them much credence."

title: Blockade succeeds where sanctions failed as Iran oil exports stall
description: , Enes Tunagur and Robert Harvey LONDON, Sept 1 (Reuters) - For the first time on record, Iran has gone about seven weeks without shipping meaningful crude exports through the Strait
fullText:
LONDON, Sept 1 (Reuters) - For the first time on record, Iran has gone about seven weeks without shipping meaningful crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz, as a U.S. naval blockade succeeds where years of sanctions ‌failed by cutting off one of Tehran's main sources of foreign-currency earnings.

Unlike previous sanctions campaigns, when Iranian crude continued reaching buyers despite restrictions, ‌the current blockade has stopped fresh crude cargoes reaching China, Tehran's only major remaining oil customer, increasing pressure on government finances and foreign-currency reserves.

Since the U.S. reinstated its blockade on Iran on ​July 14 as part of their six-month conflict, no Iranian crude cargoes have successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz to China, according to Kpler, Vortexa and TankerTrackers.com.

As a result, Iran can only sell crude to China from floating storage in Asia, which it cannot replenish as crude accumulates aboard tankers inside the strait.

"Even at the height of maximum-pressure sanctions in 2019-20, some Iranian crude cleared Hormuz every single month; at no point did outbound flows fall to near-zero for a sustained stretch ‌as they have since mid-July," Vortexa analyst Claire Jungman ⁠said.

Iran loaded about 220,000 to 255,000 barrels per day of crude oil and condensate in August, according to Vortexa and Kpler estimates, down from roughly 740,000 bpd in July and about 2 million bpd in March.

The collapse in exports is draining ⁠one of Iran's main sources of foreign-currency income and could force Tehran to finance spending by printing money, risking even higher inflation, Kpler analyst Homayoun Falakshahi said.

The International Monetary Fund estimates Iran's inflation rate at nearly 70% this year, the world's third-highest after Venezuela and Sudan.

Last week, Washington sought to increase the pressure by threatening countries that ​continue ​trading with Tehran, while stopping short of immediately imposing penalties.

US announces blockade on ‌Iran-linked Apr 13

US and Iran sign 60-day MoU, Jun 18

MoU negotiation period expires (*no circa* Aug

Iran currently has 29 tankers inside the strait carrying 36.11 million barrels of crude, TankerTrackers.com co-founder Samir Madani said.

fullText:
Sept 1 (Reuters) - UnitedHealth's insurance unit said on Tuesday that a broad range of conditions will no ‌longer need prior approval, effective October 1, as ‌it aims to eliminate prior authorization for 30% of healthcare services by ​the end of this year.

• The reduction spans a broad mix of services across multiple clinical specialties, including cardiology, genetic and laboratory testing, chiropractic care, physical, occupational ‌and speech therapy, orthopedic ⁠and musculoskeletal procedures, among others.

What additional support is being provided to rural hospitals?

What healthcare services no longer need prior authorization?

Why is UnitedHealth eliminating prior authorization requirements?

Which insurance plans are affected by these changes?

• The prior authorization requirements are being eliminated across its commercial ⁠plans, Medicare Advantage for older adults and individual insurance under the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare, and some ​other types ​of plans.

• Health insurers have ​been taking measures to ‌simplify their requirements for prior authorization on medicines and medical services after complaints from patients and doctors over excessive paperwork that can delay or even deny needed care.

• The actions are designed to reduce unnecessary paperwork, make information easier ‌to understand and allow patients and ​care providers more time to ​focus on care, UnitedHealthcare ​said.

• The company is also reducing administrative ‌requirements for eligible rural hospitals and ​affiliated providers ​through a rural prior authorization waiver program scheduled to begin on November 1.

• UnitedHealthcare is speeding payments by ​up to 50% ‌for about 1,400 rural hospitals and Critical Access Hospitals ​in the third quarter.

title: Gen Z Democratic lawmaker spars with Baby Boomers over whether American Dream is dead
description: Democratic Rep. Maxwell Frost clashed with Baby Boomers over student debt, housing prices, and whether the American dream still exists today.
fullText:
Rep. Maxwell Frost, D-Fla., engaged in a fiery debate with a group of Baby Boomers this week on the web series Surrounded, arguing that Generation Z faces economic hurdles their generation did not experience.

The 29-year-old congressman appeared in the viral debate on the Jubilee YouTube channel, where a single public figure faces an entire room of challengers.

In the debate, Frost argued that young Americans were raised with the expectation that going to college — even if it required taking on student debt — would lead to a good job, allow them to repay that debt and provide a pathway toward the American dream. He argued that this bargain, and the American dream prospect itself, no longer holds for many young Americans.

Frost cited his working-class family background and noted that he worked as an Uber driver to make ends meet while running for Congress.

Vance Warns There Will Be A Socialist President In This Country If Gop Doesn't Fix Economy For Young People

"So that's the American dream! You lived it!" his debate opponent, comedian Geno Bisconte, responded in a clip that went viral on Monday.

"The American dream isn't driving Uber to barely make ends meet," Frost replied. "The American dream is upward mobility and being able to have success."

"You went from driving an Uber to being a politician!" Bisconte shouted. "Is that upward!? What am I missing?"

"But it's not about one person. It's about the totality of a generation," Frost replied. "That's part of the reason that I have the claim that I have. The majority of my generation is struggling and having a hard time to just survive. Just to survive. The American dream isn't survival, my friend. Is the American dream survival or is it thriving? The American dream is thriving. The fact of the matter is the vast majority of young people feel like they're not able to put aside enough money to have mobility."

Another participant named William argued that many of Frost's complaints can be attributed to population growth from mass immigration.

Biden's Illegal Immigration Surge Caused Higher Rent And Home Prices, Fed Study Finds

"When we started school, there was less than 157 million people in America today. Now there's 340," William responded. "More people needing homes means home prices go up. More people needing food means food prices go up. We can't correct that until we get rid of all the foreigners that have come in here. And your party is refusing to do that, even if they're illegal!"

Frost pushed back, saying immigrants provide a net economic positive and share 

He added that entry-level wages haven't kept pace with living costs, making the prospect of buying a home on a retail or service job "a fantasy." Frost also pointed to competition in real estate, noting young buyers now face off against private equity firms.

Analysts and policy experts offered mixed takes on the generational exchange in comments to Fox News Digital.

Judge Glock, director of research and a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute, argued that in general young adults have a much higher net income than Baby Boomers did at the same age, but agreed that housing affordability is at its "worst it's been in decades." However, Glock disputed Frost's contention that institutional investors or older generations are to blame, attributing price spikes to regulatory constraints that limit new housing construction alongside high mortgage rates.

Ceo Under Fire For Mass Layoffs Amid Foreign Worker Hiring Spree Now Appointed To Fed's Task Force On Jobs

"Frost is wrong that higher housing prices are due to competition from Baby Boomers or Wall Street," Glock said. "The fundamental reason housing prices have gone up is that we are building less than we used to. And we are building less than we used to because of ever-increasing regulations, from zoning to environmental mandates. When combined with high mortgage rates due to both inflation and high levels of government debt, homeownership is becoming increasingly out of reach."

Glock also noted that "This generation also has much higher student debt levels than earlier ones. Due to their high student debt, and lack of wealth in housing, older Millennials have a lower net worth than Gen Xers at the same age. That's not because of a lack of jobs, but because colleges have been handing out ever more low-quality degrees at an ever higher cost."

Elizabeth Pipko, a former Republican National Committee national spokesperson, agreed that Gen Z faces certain major challenges, but argued they should not overestimate the luxuries the Baby Boomer generation had.

"Nobody is arguing that young Americans have it easy. And it is true that housing prices in many parts of America have risen much faster than incomes, particularly in desirable cities and suburbs. But, with that being said, times have changed and the comparison to baby boomers is not exactly fair," she said. "Households back then consumed much less. Today's family is purchasing a much higher material standard of living. What is considered 'normal' today would have been a dream to many a few decades ago. For example, the material things that improve our quality of life which were mere dreams are now not only attainable by most, but vastly cheaper. Think about computers, televisions, household technology, air travel, etc. Times have changed, yes, and with that comes difficulties, but also incredible advantages and benefits."

Click Here For More Coverage Of Media And Culture

Pipko added that immigration, artificial intelligence, and post-pandemic work shifts are compounding the tough entry-level job market for recent graduates. She cautioned against abusing H-1B visas for cheaper labor, warning that such practices put "American graduates in direct competition for the entry-level jobs that traditionally gave them their start."

Link Lauren, an influencer and former senior advisor to Robert F. Kennedy Jr., also told Fox News Digital, "For years, I've recommended trade and technical schools. If you go to college and major in queer theater or LatinX literature, don't be shocked when there aren't tons of jobs waiting for you. Unless you really need that four-year degree to go on to medical school or law school, you really have to think twice about spending all that time and money on a college campus. The American dream is certainly attainable. But the landscape has shifted. This is something Charlie Kirk spoke about often."

Fox News Digital also reached out to Frost's campaign and did not receive an immediate reply.

title: Trump says Iran is ‘DEAD’ — experts point to the real sign Tehran is nearing the brink
description: U.S. strikes on Iranian launchers near the Strait of Hormuz triggered ballistic missile retaliation as Brent crude climbed above $90 a barrel Monday.
fullText:
President Donald Trump declared Iran a "Failed Nation" Monday, claiming the country is economically and militarily broken as renewed fighting with the U.S. raises questions about how much leverage Tehran still has left.

"Iran is officially a Failed Nation. IT IS DEAD!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday morning. "They have no Navy, they have no Air Force, they have no currency, they are not paying their soldiers or police."

Trump also claimed Iranian inflation had reached 300% and said the country's leadership was "in total disarray and incapable of properly representing the country."

Iran is facing pressure from nearly every direction — renewed U.S. military strikes, tighter sanctions and a steep drop in oil exports — raising fresh questions about how long Tehran can keep absorbing the economic pain and still maintain leverage against Washington.

Could Iran's Regime Collapse? Experts Assess Bessent's Bid To Sever Financial Lifelines

Official Iranian data cited by Reuters put annual inflation at 66% in July, while the Imf projects average consumer-price inflation of 68.9% in 2026.

Trump's post came amid the sharpest U.S.-Iran military escalation in weeks. U.S. forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island Sunday after Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz, according to a U.S. official. Iran retaliated by launching ballistic missiles toward U.S. bases in Jordan, while Jordan said it intercepted eight missiles that entered its airspace.

The renewed confrontation comes as Washington ratchets up economic pressure.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters Sunday that the administration expects to roll out additional secondary sanctions as frequently as every week, initially focusing on banks and potentially cutting financial institutions that continue facilitating Iranian transactions out of the U.S. dollar-based financial system.

Iran's Deepest Weakness Is Getting Exposed Through America's Maximum Pressure Campaign

Iran's own leaders are acknowledging growing economic strain.

President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran's exports and imports have fallen nearly 35% because of U.S. sanctions and the naval blockade, while annual inflation reached 66% in July, Reuters reported Aug. 29. The IMF projects Iran's economy will contract 5.4% this year.

Miad Maleki, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies who previously served as associate director of Treasury's Office of Global Targeting at the Office of Foreign Assets Control, told Fox News Digital that the Islamic Republic may be nearing an economic breaking point. FDD says Maleki previously helped oversee U.S. sanctions programs and served as chief and senior sanctions coordinator for Iran and the Middle East.

"I think where we stand today, it's very clear — we see very clear signs, indications of what I would call an economy that is on the verge of collapse, if it hasn't already collapsed yet," Maleki said.

Maleki argued that the critical pressure point is Iran's ability to turn oil exports into usable revenue.

Us Targets Chinese Refinery In Sweeping Iran Oil Crackdown, Sanctions 'Shadow Fleet' Tankers

He estimates Tehran needs roughly 1 million barrels of oil exports per day to sustain itself, about 1.5 million to avoid hyperinflation and approximately 2 million to support development. Maleki said Iranian exports have fallen dramatically and Tehran is increasingly struggling to repatriate revenue from the oil it can sell.

Kpler data cited by Reuters showed Chinese imports of Iranian crude falling from an average 1.4 million barrels per day in 2025 to a provisional 534,000 barrels per day so far in August.

Maleki said Tehran is increasingly relying on money creation rather than cutting politically sensitive salaries and pensions. But there are limits.

"They can keep printing money, but they can't really print the type of commodities that they need, such as gasoline, such as wheat," he said.

The pressure, however, may create a dangerous paradox.

Iran Could Unleash 'Kinetic' Response As Us Tightens Economic Containment, Analyst Warns

Iran analyst Danny Citrinowicz, a fellow at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies and a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council's Scowcroft Middle East Security Initiative, told Fox News Digital that the maritime blockade, wartime losses and wider economic pressure are hurting Tehran, but argued Washington should not assume economic pain will lead to capitulation.

Citrinowicz said continued pressure could instead increase Tehran's incentive to escalate if Iranian leaders conclude the status quo is worse than renewed confrontation. He said Iran could attempt to target "U.S. economic assets in the Gulf," ports or U.S. vessels involved in enforcing the blockade, even as its missile-production capabilities have been degraded.

Maleki agreed Iran would likely attempt to escalate, but questioned how much leverage Tehran still possesses.

"They're going to try to escalate," Maleki said, pointing to the attacks of the last 24 hours. But he argued that further escalation would increasingly affect Gulf states Iran has relied upon for trade, sanctions evasion and diplomacy — potentially bringing even greater economic and diplomatic pressure.

Millions Of Barrels Of Iranian Oil Sit Beyond Trump Blockade As He Vows 'Zero Leakage'

Asked whether Iran was losing its leverage, Maleki responded: "Absolutely."

He argued Tehran has emerged weakened from internal unrest and the external war and is increasingly isolated domestically and internationally.

What Maleki is watching next is not necessarily missed government payrolls, but shortages that could trigger another wave of domestic unrest.

"What I'm looking for is shortages of items such as gasoline," Maleki said. "Right now they're fighting a war inside Iran that is way more challenging to the regime than it is from external forces that they're facing."

Commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained severely disrupted Monday, while Brent crude climbed more than 2% to above $90 as markets reacted to the renewed U.S.-Iran exchanges. Reuters reported Aug. 31 that Gulf oil flows have recovered from their wartime lows but remain below pre-war levels.

Maleki said he expects Iranians to return to the streets and argued Western governments should prepare now to help them communicate and organize if Tehran again shuts down internet access.

"What we need to do is to contain this regime, cut off this economic lifeline, empower the Iranian people, be prepared next time Iranians are back on the street [and] take actions to stop this regime from slaughtering Iranians," Maleki said.

"Those are the right policies — put the pressure on, be prepared to push back on the Iranian regime every time it escalates," he added. "At this point, they are the weakest they've been since 1979. Every time they try to escalate, they become weaker."

Original article

title: California lawmakers pass bill allowing people to identify their Jewish ancestry on state forms
description: California would allow Jews to voluntarily identify their Jewish heritage on state forms under a bill the state Legislature passed Monday.  The bill, which lawmakers sent to Gov. Gavin Newsom's desk, ...
fullText:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — California would allow Jews to voluntarily identify their Jewish heritage on state forms under a bill the state Legislature passed Monday.

The bill, which lawmakers sent to Gov. Gavin Newsom's desk, would require state agencies that collect demographic information to add "Jewish" as an option for ethnicity or ancestry. The goal is to give state officials and researchers better data on Jewish Californians, including their unemployment rates and representation in schools.

The data would enable lawmakers to create policies that address the needs of Jews in the state, said David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California, an advocacy group.

"It's about inclusion as a community," Bocarsly said, noting the Legislature has passed laws in recent years to collect more inclusive demographic data on Middle Eastern, North African and LGBTQ+ communities.

Some opponents of the bill are worried about the idea of the state collecting such data given the traumatic history of the Nazi government keeping records of Jews during the Holocaust. The proposal would bar agencies from disclosing "personal identifying information," and bill author Henry Stern, a Democratic state senator who is Jewish, said California already has robust privacy protections that should assuage those concerns.

Sydney Levy of Jewish Voice for Peace, a progressive anti-Zionist group, wasn't convinced by that argument.

"When it comes to government holding lists of Jews, we do not trust your privacy guardrails," Levy said at a hearing on the bill.

Marc Dollinger, a Jewish studies professor at San Francisco State University, said in Jewish tradition, "Jews are not supposed to be counted."

"Ultimately, it becomes a question of trust: do California Jews have confidence that this form of data collection will support and protect them or will it elevate concerns over the possible harm this sort of counting can do?" he said in an email.

Since the bill would categorize Jewish identity as an ethnicity, it could help the state track hate crimes against Jews, Dollinger said.

Levy said he also disagrees with categorizing Jews as a single ethnic group.

"Latino Jews like myself, as well as other Jews of color, have cultures and experiences different from those of white Jews," Levy said at the hearing.

Under the bill, people could still identify their race in addition to selecting "Jewish" for their ethnicity. It would be similar to how some people identify as Latino ethnically while describing their race as white, Native American or Black. The legislation was updated Friday to exempt agencies from adding "Jewish" as an option on their forms if they would for some reason lose federal funding for making the change.

Stern started wearing a kippah to work in recent years, a sign of how his relationship to his Jewish identity has evolved throughout his life.

On the same day that Hamas attacked Israel in October 2023, which launched the war in Gaza, Stern was walking to synagogue with his daughter, pushing her in a stroller, when people in a car went out of their way to yell an antisemitic remark at them, he said.

Stern was wearing a kippah. He decided to wear it regularly after that.

Stern said it was a big shift for someone who wasn't very religious as a kid, though he would be reminded that he was different from other students in junior high school, when he was bullied for being Jewish. If Stern's bill had been in place back then, it would have been a way to ensure his identity was better represented, he said.

"This bill is just trying to create a little more space for those kinds of people — just let them be seen," Stern said. "I don't think it's going to be a radical transformation. I don't think it's going to change the world."

title: He moved to Mexico after decades of being undocumented in the US. Then he got a $1.8 million fine from DHS
description: Hector “Alessandro” Negrete got the phone call nine months after he moved to Guadalajara, Mexico, hoping for a fresh start without the onerous weight of uncertainty and fear he carried in Los Angeles.
fullText:
Hector "Alessandro" Negrete got the phone call nine months after he moved to Guadalajara, Mexico, hoping for a fresh start without the onerous weight of uncertainty and fear he carried in Los Angeles.

"Hey, you have something that says, 'invoice to border patrol,'" Negrete recalls his former roommate telling him around 8 p.m. that night as he was meal-prepping after the gym. He consulted with his lawyer, and his roommate tore the envelope open.

"Vecino, what is this?" his roommate asked, calling him "neighbor" in Spanish.

Inside was a seven-digit number. He owed the Department of Homeland Security $1.8 million, the paper read.

"What the hell?" Negrete said he first thought. Perplexed, he initially believed the letter was fraudulent. He got on a FaceTime call with his roommate to process the shock.

His second thought: "Oh my God, I'm gonna lose my money. I'm gonna lose my job."

The letter sent to his old address where he still files US taxes said he must pay a $1,820,352 civil penalty for his failure to comply with a 2009 deportation order, according to a copy of the notice reviewed by CNN.

He was only 3 months old when he and his parents fled violence in their Mexican hometown and immigrated to California.

Negrete remained in the US for over 15 years after receiving a final deportation order, repeatedly trying to gain legal status but facing barriers, he said.

But after President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, 43-year-old Negrete's immigration enforcement fears and declining nonprofit work made his life in Los Angeles increasingly untenable.

"Being in a cage in LA … is not the dream that I had for my future," Negrete told CNN.

Early last year, Negrete decided to leave. He crossed into Tijuana, Mexico, by car in September 2025, before flying to Guadalajara two days later, Negrete said.

"I really genuinely felt that once I left the US, I would be done," Negrete said.

Negrete's situation is not unique. He is one of more than 100,000 undocumented immigrants who have received fines from DHS from the beginning of the second Trump administration to mid-July – amounting to more than $84 billion, DHS told CNN Monday. DHS has collected more than $1.2 million as of July 16, the agency said.

DHS warns that those who have received a final order of removal may be fined $998 per day if they don't self-deport, but the fines can be forgiven if they use the CBP Home app to leave, according to a July news release from the agency. Those who do will receive a free flight home and an "exit bonus of $2,600."

"Our message is clear: illegal aliens in the country unlawfully should leave now or face consequences—including financial penalties," DHS said in a statement to CNN.

Charles Moore, a senior attorney at legal nonprofit Public Justice – which is suing the federal government for the immigration fines – said DHS is imposing penalties on people who may be complying with immigration requirements or pursuing lawful routes to remain in the country.

"This administration is weaponizing these fines to terrorize families and to push immigrants out of the country," Moore said.

The federal government has argued the fine program was authorized by statutes passed by Congress nearly 30 years ago and is lawful.

"Whether an alien remains in country to pursue other forms of immigration relief is not a defense under the statutes," the government said in a January court filing.

DHS referred CNN to the Treasury and Justice departments when reached for additional information.

Negrete and his lawyers twice provided evidence that he was living in Mexico, but officials demanded additional documentation, he and his attorney Marissa Montes said. Now Negrete – who works remotely for a US-based international nonprofit fighting ageism – is worried the government could pursue his US income and is considering joining litigation challenging the fines.

Negrete, born in Mexico in 1982, settled with his family first in South Los Angeles and later grew up primarily on Los Angeles' east side in Boyle Heights.

Negrete spent a month in Mexico when he was around 6 years old. During his return trip back to the US, a woman hired to bring him across the border held him for more than a week and demanded additional money from his family, Negrete said. He described being tied in a vehicle and confined at her home.

"By the second night, I stopped crying as much because, at that young age, I guess I was just like, well, this is my new life," he said.

Negrete did not discover his immigration status until after graduating from high school, he recounted.

Negrete said he had been accepted to the University of California, Berkeley, but learned he did not have a Social Security number while applying for scholarships.

"I remember asking my mom, like, 'Oh, where's my Social?' … It was just a huge shock of confusion."

Unable to afford college, he began working to help support his mother.

"I worked hard my entire life up to that point, and I couldn't do anything. I couldn't go to college," Negrete said. "I didn't know how to feel angry because I didn't know who to be angry at."

Negrete says he repeatedly tried to obtain legal status: First through his father, who became a lawful permanent resident after marrying a US citizen. But that effort failed because his father had accidentally omitted him from an immigration form, he said. A DUI conviction in 2008 had prevented Negrete from initially applying for Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) in 2012, though his record was eventually expunged, Montes told CNN. He then started the DACA application process before new applications were halted by the Trump administration in 2017, he said.

At the time, undocumented status was discussed through "shame or secrecy," he recalled.

Negrete later became open about his status and got involved in immigrant rights and social justice work. He was a neighborhood council member and described himself as a "Dreamer," although Negrete never received DACA status.

"Learning to tell my story from a place of resilience over fear was something that I needed to practice," Negrete said.

Negrete built a career in nonprofits and philanthropy and became an openly undocumented and queer community advocate.

Negrete first considered leaving the US during Trump's first term but said he stayed after his mother was diagnosed with cancer in late 2017.

Then came the second Trump administration. Negrete had lost work and tried drawing on savings before concluding that remaining in the US was no longer financially sustainable. He didn't want to spend four years hiding or continue living with uncertainty over detention and removal, he explained.

"It wasn't even fear of being deported. It was more the in-between space," he said.

He had already decided to leave the US when immigration operations and protests in Los Angeles intensified in June 2025. He spent much of that summer indoors, too scared to go to the gym or engage in his usual activities. Then, he began saying his goodbyes.

"I didn't want to live in a cage," he said.

Before leaving, Negrete played in a final softball tournament in Sacramento. The week before, he held a yard sale and going-away party where friends bought most of his belongings – like his scary movie memorabilia collection – as keepsakes.

He gave guests cards with the message: "A new home, different door, same key."

Months before leaving, Negrete shared the same sentiment in a "love letter" on Substack.

"After over 40 years of living in Los Angeles, a city that shaped me, strengthened me, and loved me back, I've decided to repatriate politically back to Mexico," he wrote. "But let me be absolutely clear: this is not goodbye to LA, but rather a rebirth for me, and hopefully for some of you too."

Negrete stuffed one large suitcase with coats and professional clothes, along with a smaller bag with his dog's things. He said he left Los Angeles on September 4, 2025, and drove about three and a half hours on Interstate 5. Accompanied by friends and his dog, Negrete crossed the border into Tijuana, he remembered.

On the way, Negrete and his friends stopped at a beach for a spiritual ceremony. They spent the rest of the drive talking, and one of his friends pleaded, "It's not too late; we can turn back," Negrete recounted.

Negrete said he tried to "keep it together," but he broke down that night in Tijuana when his friends shared a heartfelt video they made him – whom they lovingly referred to as "Ale." A photo slideshow played and friends shared farewell messages on camera saying they would miss "the glue to our group."

The next day, he took a one-way flight to Guadalajara, Negrete said, feeling anxious as he traveled farther into Mexico.

"What am I doing leaving this very comfortable, uncomfortable place?" Negrete remembered thinking. His friends dropped him off "like I was in college."

Negrete described the move as emotionally painful yet ultimately empowering.

But the culture shock kicked in swiftly: Although he was among the strongest Spanish speakers in his US social circle, he initially struggled with Guadalajara's local dialect, he joked. Finding housing proved to be another hurdle. It took him around four months to obtain Mexican identification and a tax number.

"I really had to navigate everything from being a tourist," Negrete said.

He described having lingering anxiety around law enforcement: Seeing police initially triggered worry conditioned by his years living without status in the US, though later he had begun to feel safer in Mexico.

"I'm like, wait, I'm fine. I'm good," he said.

But back in Los Angeles, the life he thought he had escaped nearly a year prior came back to haunt him: the massive fine.

Dated May 5, the fine cites the Immigration and Nationality Act Section 274D(a), which authorizes DHS to impose monetary penalties on any noncitizen who "willfully fails or refuses to depart from the United States" after a final order of removal.

The notice says "If immigration officials can verify your departure, and if you are otherwise eligible for the debt rescission program, the United States will rescind the debt listed above."

Negrete's lawyers responded twice, but DHS dismissed their appeal and requested more evidence, according to his attorney and a notice reviewed by CNN.

"There was ample proof that Alessandro self-deported," Montes said. "We provided that proof to the government, and even then, they said it wasn't sufficient."

Negrete said his lawyers had immediately responded to the initial letter, barely meeting the 15-day deadline for an appeal.

The appeal was filed on May 20 and the government denied it on June 2, his lawyers said. A day later, the government sent another invoice with the penalty and gave Negrete 10 days to appeal through email. Negrete responded on June 12, providing additional evidence he lives in Mexico, to which DHS responded that he didn't submit enough evidence.

The fact that Negrete drove into Tijuana rather than flying directly from Los Angeles complicated documentation of his exit, Montes said. His attorneys say they submitted evidence that he left the country: signed declarations from a friend and reporter, his lease agreement in Guadalajara, domestic plane tickets within Mexico, a news article documenting his move and his Mexican ID documents.

Now, his legal team is preparing another submission that will include a passport stamp from another country.

The department also asked him to record his departure through the CBP Home app, but Negrete said he has not done so yet because he is concerned about how that information might be used.

DHS had said in the July release that by using the CBP Home app, "illegal aliens earn forgiveness for any civil fines or penalties for failing to depart the country."

In July, two US senators sent a letter to the administration demanding the fines be halted, saying it has "abused" its authorities under the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigration Responsibility Act "in an attempt to frighten immigrants—many of whom are seeking a green card or who have maintained lawful presence in the United States for decades."

A lawsuit challenging the DHS fines was filed last November in Massachusetts on behalf of two women, proceeding under the pseudonyms Maria L. and Nancy M.

The lead attorney, Moore, said regulatory changes adopted in June 2025 removed several protections for fine recipients, which DHS said would "make it easier and more efficient to fine illegal aliens."

Recipients previously had 30 days to respond and could request an extension; now they have 15 business days, the rule says.

Immigrants also previously received a "notice of intention to fine," but the current notice is described as a "notice of violation and order." Extensions and in-person interviews are unavailable, and the appeals process for the penalties has been transferred from an appeals board to DHS, according to the rule. The revisions also removed the ability to ask DHS to rescind a penalty after a final decision is made, so a person who later becomes a lawful permanent resident may remain liable for the fine, Moore said. DHS, however, can reopen decisions at any time to reconsider and reduce or rescind fines, according to the rule.

The notices do not adequately explain what conduct allegedly violated the law and the size of the fines violates the Constitution's prohibition against excessive fines, the lawsuit in Massachusetts alleges.

Moore argues the fines are being used to financially and psychologically pressure immigrants to leave the US and the government is not adequately considering whether a person "willfully" failed to depart, as required by law.

The federal government has noted officials still make an individual determination of whether a person's conduct was willful or voluntary, according to the January court filing.

CNN has reached out to the Department of Justice for comment.

A fine of $1.8 million appears to be among the most common penalty amounts, representing $998 a day over five years, Moore said.

About 70% of surveyed attorneys of $998-per-day fine recipients say their clients had obtained or were pursuing lawful status, according to an August report from the New York University School of Law's Immigrant Rights Clinic. Like Negrete, over half had resided in the US for at least a decade after receiving their final deportation order.

Moore said the court held a hearing July 22 on the plaintiffs' request for a stay, which would prevent the government from imposing or enforcing the fines in the challenged manner while litigation proceeds. The judge is now considering that motion, and a ruling is expected in the coming weeks or months, Moore said.

Because Negrete works for US clients and pays US taxes using an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number, he worries authorities could garnish his wages or take other collection measures, he said.

The government has filed over 50 lawsuits against fine recipients as of May, according to the NYU report. If successful, they could then garnish their wages, place a lien on their property or freeze funds in their bank accounts, the report states. By law and regulation, the federal government can also utilize administrative wage garnishment without a ruling in a collections suit, the report states.

The fines primarily affect working-class people who could never afford to pay the fine, the report said.

Montes said it remains unclear how the government intends to collect the penalties or whether it could garnish Negrete's US-sourced wages.

Negrete is now saving more money and paying his rent in advance to ensure he has housing if the dispute interrupts his income.

He does not plan to move back to the US, but he does hope to eventually visit loved ones after a 10-year reentry bar expires, he said. His mother lives in Denver, and his father and most of his siblings are in Pomona, California. Because his parents have legal status and his siblings are US citizens, they can visit him instead.

Though he does not regret leaving, Negrete said getting legal advice might have changed how he approached his departure. After moving, Negrete's lawyers told him his childhood trafficking experience might have provided a route to lawful status.

"I still believe that I made the best decision that I thought for myself in the moment," Negrete said.

He said moving to Mexico has allowed him to travel and consider buying property – possibilities he could not imagine in Los Angeles.

But Negrete and Montes strongly urge undocumented people considering departure from the US to consult an immigration attorney first, investigate all potential relief and understand the consequences of leaving.

His advice to others: "Talk to a lawyer…Definitely don't do it the way that I did."

There are countless things Negrete says he misses about LA: his "chosen family," playing with his softball team, running with the Boyle Heights Bridge Runners on Wednesdays and downtown nightlife on weekends.

"But I don't miss living under persecution," he said.

title: The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Are Aura Battles?
description: From battling for aura points to weaponized body odor, here is your guide to the youth trends of the week.
fullText:
This week's trip into the culture of young people is filled with bad ideas and stupidity, but it's that specific kind of stupidity that's the sole purview of youth—unserious, frequently baffling, but ultimately harmless. Old people are just as stupid, but our stupidity has consequences. Debating whether ditching basic hygiene to be more attractive is dumb as dirt, but it's not going to crash the housing market, and no one really dies in an aura battle. So here's what's going on with the young people and what it all means.

To Gens Z and A, "aura" is, essentially, coolness or charisma ("rizz" if you prefer). An "aura battle" is a public contest in which the person with the most aura, as determined by crowd and/or comment section reaction, is the winner. It's a little like a breakdance or rap battle, but without the talent.

The trend seems to have originated in Latin America in the beginning of 2026 and quickly spread worldwide. It's recently come to the U.S. Here's Mr. Poo Poo and Latavious Quavious squaring off this past weekend in NYC at what was billed as the "first-ever American aura championship."

I've been watching Aura Battles for the last hour or so, just to see if I can determine what adds up to "aura," and I got nothing—it seems like most of the "battle" is doing bad versions of meme dances. But I'm not dismissing aura battles; the first breakdance battles were probably pretty rough too, and anything that gets kids outside and hanging out with each other is cool.

It's unlikely, but aura battles could develop into an organic artistic expression of the soul of the younger generation. If so, the video below is history being made, the equivalent of the first time Cool Herc set up two turntables to play break beats. Ladies and gentlemen, here is the final round of the first-ever American aura battle championship.

(I feel like Applewood got robbed, tbh.)

Police departments, school districts, and other authority figures from Baltimore to Donegal are sounding the alarm over a terrifying new trend of...kids posting memes about The Cat in the Hat.

The often AI-generated videos cropping up on TikTok and the like feature someone dressed as the famous cartoon cat and cryptic warnings. They sometimes include scary music. This has led to online rumors that there's a Cat in the Hat serial killer on the loose. There isn't, but the trend did lead to an incident that's at least a little real. In Constantine, Mich., a user called "catinthehat" reportedly issued threats against specific students, prompting state police and the FBI to get involved.

Still, authorities all over the world locking down schools, stepping up police patrols, and threatening to arrest people over a meme seems more than a little silly. I get that school shootings are scary, but maybe shrugging at the easy availability of firearms and freaking out over Cat in the Hat memes isn't the best approach to stopping them?

Completing this week's triptych of idiocy is "pheromone maxxing." -Maxxing, as I'm sure you know, is doing something a lot. Pheromones are chemicals that some animals release that influence the behavior of other members of their species, so pheromone maxxing is trying to influence the behaviors of others through your stink. Supposedly, young men in the "looksmaxxing" community are skipping showers and not washing their clothing in an attempt to make young women like them more. It's difficult to determine how widespread the belief is, but there are at least a few would-be influencers unironically advocating for the practice, although the vast majority's online response is basically, "ew."

So is there anything to it? While humans do produce chemical odors in response to emotional states, they aren't actually "pheromones" like in the animal world, and the number of smelly, single men at comic book conventions provides strong corollary evidence that not showering is a bad strategy for attracting potential mates. On the other hand, there's this guy's TikTok, where he reports he stopped using cologne and started getting more and more compliments. I believe him, because can you imagine how horrible his cologne was?

Lesbian Space Princess is a (barely) animated 2025 movie from Australia. Written and directed by Emma Hough Hobbs and Leela Varghese, and according to some online, it's bringing about world peace.

LSP tells the story of Princess Saira from the planet Clitopolis and her battle with the Straight White Maliens. Even though it has a critical rating of 98% on Rotten Tomatoes, it wasn't well-known outside of Australia. But recently, people started posting clips of the movie online. Because everyone (except critics, apparently) thinks it's bad.

Right-wing people hate-post LSP as an example of "overly woke" media; lefties hate-post it because it's so on-the-nose and terminally online that it's painfully unfunny. Fans of Hazbin Hotel post about LSP because it's way worse than their favorite franchise. So do Marvel fanboys. Before long, Memes like this—

—started popping up featuring the phrase "Just this Once," as fandoms realized that they at least share this one thing in common. The Great Truce of 2026 is bringing Naruto and One Piece fans together. Football fans are coming together with futbol fans. It's so widespread, the belief is growing that Lesbian Space Princess badness is so complete that it's bringing about world peace.

title: Wales select eight uncapped players in WXV squad
description: Wales include eight uncapped players in squad for the WXV Global Series games against South Africa and USA in Cardiff.
fullText:
Wales head coach Sean Lynn has named eight uncapped players in his 39-strong squad for this month's WXV Global Series fixtures.

Back-row forwards Alex Callender and Kate Williams are co-captains for the Tests against South Africa and USA at Cardiff Arms Park.

They are joined in the squad by wings Amy Williams and Kelsie Webster and prop Stella Orrin, who played in June's uncapped game against the Barbarians at Twickenham.

Five other Test novices are included – props Crystal James and Elan Jones, hooker Shanelle Williams, scrum half Megan Davey and centre Hanna Tudor.

Head coach Lynn said: "This selection underlines how hard the players, coaches and staff have worked, and we are seeing competition for places really develop in the squad."

Wales pushing the pain barrier in bid to improve

Neumann joins Leicester Tigers after Quins exit

Callender will aim to win her first cap since the 2025 World Cup after missing the Six Nations through injury while fellow influential back-rower Kate Williams was also sidelined for the final three rounds of the championship.

Wales open their campaign against South Africa on Friday, 18 September (19:15 BST) and host USA on Saturday, 26 September (15:00 BST).

Lynn's side then go to Tokyo to face Japan on Friday, 23 October (16:00 BST) before moving on to Kumagaya for a second Test on Saturday, 31 October (07:00 BST).

All three opponents are ranked above Wales, who have dropped to 12th in the world after nine consecutive Test defeats.

But they did end their losing streak against the Barbarians at Twickenham in June when Lynn was given food for thought after fielding an inexperienced side.

"We have really moved the dial during the first three weeks of pre-season with the fitness and the rugby sessions demanding more from the squad," he said.

"The players have really pushed each other and to witness how that is driving standards in training is the reason why we have selected the squad size we have."

Wales intend to hold a probables versus possibles training game to help with their selection for the South Africa opener.

Lynn named an extended 46-player training squad in August and then added half-back Megan Davey.

Lily Hawkins, Ffion Williams, Savannah Picton Powell, Hannah Marshall, Molly Wakely, Tilly Vucaj, Lucy Isaac and Anwen Owen miss out for the Cardiff fixtures.

title: McMenamin joins Glens two months after Coleraine move
description: Northern Ireland international Conor McMenamin makes a shock switch from Coleraine to Glentoran, which comes just two months after he signed for the Bannsiders.
fullText:
Northern Ireland international Conor McMenamin has made a shock switch from Coleraine to Glentoran just two months after he signed for the Bannsiders.

As part of the deal, Joe Thomson will make the move to the Showgrounds from Coleraine on a two-year deal.

Winger McMenamin signed for Coleraine on 23 June in a high-profile move as he returned to the Irish Premiership after three years in the SPL with St Mirren.

The 31-year-old, who has struggled with a number of injuries over the past two seasons, did not start a game during his brief spell with Coleraine.

Billed as a key member of Ruaidhri Higgins' star-studded attack with the likes of Matthew Shevlin, Ben Doherty and Joel Cooper, McMenamin's move back to Glentoran is a shock transfer.

Speaking about the player's departure, Higgins said: "These things happen in football and I've no personal issue with Conor whatsoever.

"Initially part of the plan is that he'd move closer to the north coast which hasn't happened.

"I think when you do that commute from Downpatrick to Coleraine and back every day, I think it can have a negative impact on your body.

"I didn't think it was ideal, neither did Conor after a few good conversations, and we've decided to come to this arrangement which I think suits all parties."

It is a third spell at the Oval for McMenamin, who had a season at the east Belfast side in 2015-16 and then a stand-out two years from 2021 until 2023, which led to his move to Scotland.

He won the first of his 14 Northern Ireland caps in 2022 while still at Glentoran, and scored against San Marino the following year.

However, he has not featured under manager Michael O'Neill since a late cameo in the 5-1 defeat by Spain in June 2024.

"Everything has happened really quickly, but once I knew there was an opportunity to return to Glentoran, I was delighted to take it," said McMenamin.

He added: "I played some of the best football of my career here, earned my first Northern Ireland call-up and secured a move to Scotland. My three years with St Mirren were hugely important and I return as a better and more experienced player.

"This is not about looking back at what I achieved here before. I still have plenty that I want to accomplish."

McMenamin is Glentoran's sixth signing of the summer, following the arrivals of Zeno Ibsen Rossi, Greg Sloggett, Rhys Walsh, Lekan Sule and Ethan Schilte-Brown, with Walsh having since joined Annagh United.

Coleraine top the Irish Premiership table with three wins and a draw from four matches, while Glentoran are sixth with two wins and two defeats in a mixed start to their campaign.

title: Boss Goodwin leaves hospital but still absent from Dundee Utd role
description: Dundee United manager Jim Goodwin has been released from hospital after a health scare but it remains unclear when he will resume his duties.
fullText:
Dundee United manager Jim Goodwin has been released from hospital after a health scare but it remains unclear when he will resume his duties.

Goodwin, 44, missed United's 4-0 Scottish Premiership win at Kilmarnock on Saturday after taking ill and being admitted to hospital last Thursday.

Assistant Lee Sharp took the team at Rugby Park, and will do so again for United's midweek trip to play Motherwell amid the Irishman's continued absence.

"He is out of hospital, he is back home recovering," Sharp said of Goodwin. "He is waiting on direction from the doctors etc to where he goes from there."

Asked if there was any indication when Goodwin would return, Sharp replied: "No. He would be back just now if he was allowed. We are in constant dialogue so he will let me know as soon as."

In Goodwin's absence, it remains business as usual at United, with the club closing on a move to bring former Dundee midfielder Lyall Cameron to Tannadice on loan from Rangers.

title: Beckham and Mourinho pay tribute to Messi
description: Former England captain Sir David Beckham says Lionel Messi has inspired "millions of children worldwide," following the Argentine retiring from international football.
fullText:
Former England captain Sir David Beckham says Lionel Messi has inspired "millions of children worldwide" and his "legacy will live forever" following the Argentine's retirement from international football.

Beckham, co-owner of Messi's club Inter Miami, paid tribute to the 39-year-old's international career in which he scored 125 goals in 207 games.

Messi captained Argentina to World Cup glory in Qatar in 2022, saw them reach the final again in 2026 and won two Copa America titles in 2021 and 2024.

"This is the moment we get to look back on and realize how grateful we were to witness the greatness of a young kid with a dream," Beckham said on Instagram.

"Leo, you delivered the greatest gift to your country and, for that, your legacy will live forever. Congratulations on all you achieved for Argentina."

Real Madrid manager Jose Mourinho commented on Messi's retirement post on Instagram, saying "the next Copa America and the next World Cup won't be the same," without Messi involved.

Mourinho frequently managed against Messi in his first stint at Real Madrid between 2010 and 2013, a period in which the former Barcelona man won the Ballon d'Or in three consecutive years (2010-2012).

Former Argentina midfielder Angel di Maria, who also played alongside Messi at Paris St-Germain, described him as "the greatest of all time".

"All I know is that I was born in the right century to be able to witness you play, relish your performances and, on top of that, share all those years with you in the national team," he added.

Fellow Argentina World Cup winning team-mate and ex-Spurs defender Cristian Romero posted: "As a kid, I dreamed of meeting you someday. But I never imagined that life would give me the gift of sharing this with you and living by your side through the golden age and greatest era of our national team."

Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez shared a similar dream of playing with Messi "even just once," adding: "Life ended up being far more beautiful than that boy was able to imagine.

"I didn't just get to play with you, but we shared training camps, the dressing room, the conversations, the embraces, the difficult moments, the wonderful moments, and we ended up world champions together."

Fifa president Gianni Infantino said: "Congratulations on an extraordinary international career which has inspired millions and redefined the beautiful game.

"Thank you for every unforgettable memory while wearing the colors of [Argentina] and for uniting fans across every corner of the globe."

Commenting on Messi's instagram post, Argentinian Formula One driver Franco Colapinto said: "There are no words that will ever be enough to express our gratitude.

"Thank you for getting back up time and time again and giving everything to make an entire country happy. You are an example to all of us."

title: Portsmouth goalkeeper legend Knight dies aged 65
description: Goalkeeper Alan Knight, who played 801 Portsmouth games, dies aged 65 after being diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2024.
fullText:
Former Portsmouth goalkeeper Alan Knight has died aged 65 after being diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2024.

Knight spent 22 years playing at Fratton Park, making 801 appearances between 1978 and 2000 – the record for a keeper at a single English club.

Pompey fans gave him the nickname The Legend and after retiring he became both a coach and ambassador for the club.

In a moving tribute to their former player, a club statement, external said: "The word legend is often overused in football, but the fact that Alan was still known as The Legend at Pompey more than 20 years after hanging up his gloves speaks volumes.

"He will be sadly missed by the Fratton faithful, team-mates and all of us at the club who knew and loved him.

"Our thoughts are with Alan's wife Heather, his daughters Jade and Rebekah and all his family and friends at this incredibly sad time. Rest in peace, The Legend".

Portsmouth captain Marlon Pack posted on social media: "RIP Knightsie. A true club legend who bled blue. A figure who has done so much for this football club and the wider community over so many years".

Knight kept a clean sheet on his debut, aged 16, against Rotherham in the old Division Three in 1978 and he went on to represent the club in all four divisions.

There were three promotion-winning campaigns, including a Division Three title success and Pompey's return to top-flight football for the first time in 28 years in the 1986-87 season.

Knight's final appearance for the club came aged 38 on 3 January 2000 in a 2-1 Division One defeat at Norwich, making him the only Blues player to have played across four decades.

Knight was awarded an MBE following his retirement, and was also handed the Freedom of the City of Portsmouth.

Portsmouth legend Knight reveals cancer diagnosis

'Football helped me through my cancer diagnosis'

Speaking to the BBC following his cancer diagnosis, Knight said it "came as a massive shock" but he wanted to discuss it publicly to encourage others to seek advice if they spot symptoms.

He joined a group of men playing walking football in Portsmouth and said it helped them all come to terms with their diagnoses.

"Once you get diagnosed, once the cancer word is used, it just changes everything," he said.

"The support network, having your mates around you - family first and foremost - but then to have your mates and your team-mates around you is huge.

"It gives you that lift when you can be slipping into that bit of depression."

title: Stokes to play for Adelaide Strikers in Big Bash
description: Former England captain Ben Stokes joins Adelaide Strikers for the 2026-27 season of the Big Bash League.
fullText:
Former England captain Ben Stokes has joined Adelaide Strikers for the 2026-27 season of the T20 Big Bash League.

The 35-year-old made the shock decision to retire from international cricket in June, with the announcement coming during the third and final Test of a 2-1 home series defeat against New Zealand.

Stokes played 122 Tests, 114 one-day internationals and 43 T20s for England.

He scored a superb 84 in the final against New Zealand when England dramatically won the World Cup for the first time in 2019.

"I'm really excited to be joining the Adelaide Strikers for BBL 16," said Stokes.

"I've always enjoyed playing in Australia, and when the opportunity came up to join the Strikers it was one I couldn't pass up.

"Adelaide Oval is an incredible place to play cricket, the Big Bash is a fantastic competition and the Strikers have an exciting group, so I'm looking forward to meeting the players, getting stuck in and contributing to a successful season.

"I can't wait to get started, create some special memories with the group and give Strikers fans plenty to cheer about."

Adelaide said Stokes, who had a brief stint at fellow BBL side Melbourne Renegades in 2015, would be available for the whole of the BBL 16 campaign, which starts in December.

"Ben is one of the greatest all-rounders the game has seen, a proven match-winner and a competitor who thrives under pressure," said Adelaide Strikers head coach Tim Paine, whose side start their BBL season against Sydney Thunder on 16 December.

"We're thrilled to have a player of his ability join our squad and can't wait to see him put on a show in BBL 16."

title: GB's Fery returns to Grand Slam stage - what lies ahead?
description: Shock Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery returns to the Grand Slam stage when he faces Italy's Lorenzo Musetti at the US Open.
fullText:
As the top stars congregated in New York for last year's US Open, Arthur Fery was looking in from the outside.

The Briton had just crept back inside the world's top 300 after winning an ATP Challenger event in Colombia and admits it was a "bit painful" watching players at the pinnacle of the sport.

Twelve months on, the 24-year-old is rubbing shoulders with the elite at Flushing Meadows, thanks to the stunning run to the Wimbledon semi-finals which has likely changed his life forever.

Fery's career is certainly unrecognisable compared to where it was.

He starts his US Open debut against Italian 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti on Tuesday as the 33rd-ranked player in the world, the British men's number one and a recent first-time finalist on the ATP Tour.

On watching the US Open from afar last year, Fery said: "It's a little bit painful seeing all the guys your age who you were playing with in juniors playing the US Open - and you're playing Challengers.

"You don't really want to be too stuck on other guys' results or watching matches. You want to focus on yourself.

"That's what I've been trying to do and now that I'm doing well, it's a little bit easier. You feel 

Wawrinka feels the love on Grand Slam goodbye

GB's Fearnley and Dart complete superb comeback wins

During his time as a professional, Fery has always carried himself with an air of assurance.

Although his extraordinary Wimbledon performance was unexpected, it feels he has the temperament to take the new experiences it has brought in his stride.

His debut at ATP Masters level ended in a win over Australia's James Duckworth at the Cincinnati Open, although the speed and guile of world number eight Alex de Minaur proved too much in the next round.

From there Fery travelled to North Carolina, where he finished runner-up at the ATP 250 event in Winston-Salem.

While he lost to higher-ranked Peruvian Ignacio Buse in Saturday's final, Fery says his four victories - albeit against opponents a Grand Slam semi-finalist would be expected to beat - have enhanced his sense of belonging.

"It was a very positive week for me. Obviously there is nowhere near as much attention as the Slams and big ATP events, but I've got to remind myself that its not a normal thing yet to make ATP 250 finals," Fery told BBC Sport.

"I wasn't really happy with my match in the final, but it was a long week and first time I'd played five matches in five days in a very long time.

"It's great preparation for the US Open."

Taking a month off tour after Wimbledon was another strategic move designed to help Fery flourish in the tail-end of the season.

The run scuppered an already-booked holiday to Greece, but a rearranged lads' trip to Spain - which included plenty of time on the golf course - provided the chance to recover from suddenly finding himself in the global spotlight.

"I was able to get some time off with friends and family, go on holiday and enjoy the success I'd had with them," he said.

"I'm happy with taking that amount of time off and even though I had to practise a little bit longer to get back into the flow of things, it was really worth it - mainly from a mental standpoint."

To Wimbledon and back - Fery's voyage to Centre Court spotlight

Fery narrowly missed out on a seeding at the US Open, which are given to the top 32 players, leaving him vulnerable to drawing one of the leading stars in New York.

Musetti, who is an excellent returner and slick mover, must be counted among the title favourites in a wide open men's draw.

A quarter-finalist in New York last year, the 25-year-old has gone a step further at both the French Open and Wimbledon in the recent seasons, and reached the Australian Open last eight in January.

A thigh injury ruled him out of the French Open and Wimbledon, but he has showed signs of rediscovering his best level in recent runs to the Washington and Cincinnati quarter-finals.

"Some weeks you get good draws, some weeks you get tougher draws - it is how it is," said Fery.

"I missed out by one spot on a seeded position and then I draw the 13th seed - it's a bit unfortunate but some things go your way and some things don't.

"I still feel I have my chances in that match-up if I prepare and play well."

Whatever happens against Musetti, it will be intriguing to see how Fery fares over the coming months given his new-found status.

There has already been plenty of discussion about whether the 5ft 9in Londoner's stature will be a limiting factor on an ATP Tour where taller players tend to thrive.

"I don't think Arthur's height has to be something which we sit here and worry about," says Michael Bourne, the Lawn Tennis Association's performance director.

"He has great ball speed – whether off the ground or from the serve, he's an amazing decision-maker and a very good athlete.

title: Brighton agree £15m deal for Millwall winger Azeez
description: Brighton agree a deal to sign 25-year-old Nigeria winger Femi Azeez from Championship club Millwall.
fullText:
Brighton have agreed a deal to sign Nigeria winger Femi Azeez from Millwall.

The 25-year-old scored 11 goals and provided eight assists in 37 games last season, earning a place in the PFA Championship team of the year.

Azeez has been pushing for a move to the Premier League, with Millwall rejecting at least three bids from the Seagulls in recent weeks.

His departure would be a club record sale for Millwall, who are set to receive an initial £12.5m - potentially rising past £15m with add-ons.

Azeez would be Brighton's 11th signing of the summer, including their club record £45m move for Tottenham centre-back Luka Vuskovic.

The Seagulls have also raised significant funds through player sales, including Carlos Baleba's £70m move to Manchester United, while Liverpool have been linked with winger Yankuba Minteh.

Azeez joined Millwall from Reading for about £1m in 2024 and is entering the final two years of his contract.

He had been left out of the Lions' three most recent matchday squads by manager Alex Neil.

Fellow Championship club Wrexham are also understood to have shown an interest in Azeez.

His arrival at Brighton will allow Seagulls winger Amario Cozier-Duberry, who has signed a new contract, to leave on loan.

The 21-year-old, who had a successful loan spell at Bolton Wanderers in League One last season, is expected to join Championship side Middlesbrough this term.

He looks likely to replace Morgan Whittaker at Boro, with the winger set to join Major League Soccer side Colorado Rapids.

title: Hull sign Ansah and close on Norton-Cuffy
description: Hull City sign forward Ilyas Ansah on a five-year deal from Bundesliga side Union Berlin.
fullText:
Hull City have signed forward Ilyas Ansah from Union Berlin and agreed a £12m deal for Genoa right-back Brooke Norton-Cuffy.

English full-back Cody Drameh, who has featured in all three of Hull's games this season, is heading in the opposite direction to Norton-Cuffy - with Genoa set to pay £3.4m.

Norton-Cuffy, 22, who has spent two years with the Serie A side, began his career at Arsenal and was part of the England Under-21 squad that retained the European Championship in Slovakia in 2025.

Germany Under-21 international Ansah joins Hull on a five-year contract for a reported fee of 15m euros (£12.8m) with 12m euros (£10.2m) in add-ons.

He becomes the 13th player to arrive at Hull this summer, with the club having won their first two matches since returning to the Premier League after a nine-year absence.

"I'm very excited. It's a dream come true for me to play in the Premier League, and for such a big club - it's really an honour for me," Ansah said.

"I have heard a lot about the club, the players and the team, and I'm excited to play with the boys and to get to know them.

"I'm definitely a player who always gives his best and leaves it all on the pitch."

The 6ft 4in forward, who turns 22 in November, scored five goals in 36 matches in all competitions for Union Berlin last term.

They are also in advanced talks to sign 19-year-old Olympiacos midfielder Christos Mouzakitis for about £13m.

title: Ski Sunday to end after nearly 50 years
description: The BBC is to end its Ski Sunday programme after nearly 50 years.
fullText:
Ski Sunday, the BBC's winter sports programme, is to end after nearly 50 years.

First broadcast in 1978, it featured the best of winter sports action, with Ed Leigh and Chemmy Alcott its most recent presenting team.

"Changing audience behaviours and the tough financial decisions needed to meet savings requirements mean BBC Sport must continually review how it delivers value for licence fee payers and serves audiences across all platforms. This decision forms part of that process," said a BBC Sport statement.

Philip Bernie, head of BBC Sport events, said Ski Sunday "has been a truly iconic programme".

He added: "Generations of viewers have enjoyed its coverage of the best in winter sports.

"We are enormously proud of the role it has played in bringing these moments to audiences across the UK, and extremely grateful to the brilliant people who have delivered them, not least the current outstanding team.

"These decisions are never easy, but as audience viewing habits evolve and we work to deliver value for licence fee payers, we have to make tough choices.

"We remain committed to bringing audiences the very best of winter sport, above all at the Winter Olympics, across BBC Sport's platforms."

title: Palace and Sunderland battling for £30m Fofana

fullText:
Crystal Palace are attempting to hijack Sunderland's move for Lyon's Malick Fofana.

The winger had agreed to join Sunderland in a deal worth just under £30m but Palace have made their own proposal.

It is now up to the the 21-year-old to decide as he travels to England for a medical, having been offered a five-year contract at the Stadium of Light.

Any deal for the Belgium forward would cost an initial £25.6m, with a potential £4.3m in add-ons.

Fofana was understood to be excited by the prospect of joining Sunderland before their first European campaign in 51 years, having qualified for the Europa League, but Palace have also qualified for the same competition.

Arsenal also attempted to sign Fofana, but the Premier League champions were unable to agree a fee with Lyon.

Fofana began his career at KAA Gent before joining the Ligue 1 side in 2024.

If he joins Sunderland, Fofana would sign alongside Kevin Danso, with the Austria defender due to arrive from Tottenham on an initial loan with an option to buy.

Sunderland have also signed defenders Thomas Meunier and Dayann Methalie, and midfielder Jules Ahoka, this summer after finishing seventh in their first season back in the top flight.
