description: Thousands of cases of tofu that were sold in 29 states have been recalled.
fullText:
Thousands of cases of tofu have been recalled in dozens of states over possible chemical contamination.

According to a recent report from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, some pre-cooked tofu distributed by hodo has been recalled because they could be contaminated with ink.

The affected products were sent to 29 states across the country and have use by dates through November.

The recall, which was initiated on Aug. 7, applies to more than 10,000 cases of tofu.

USA TODAY has reached out to hodo for comment.

Check your grill brush: 3.6 million recalled

More than 10,000 cases of hodo's Lightly Fried Chili Crisp Tofu have been recalled. The affected products have a net weight of 8 ounces and are kept refrigerated.

The products have a UPC code of 850565007842, according to the FDA report.

The affected products have best if used by dates spanning from May to November. The full list of products that may still be lingering in fridges is below:

Lot code 260423 with use by date 08/22/2026

Lot code 260521 with use by date 09/19/2026

Lot code 260611 with use by date 10/10/2026

Lot code 260625 with use by date 10/24/2026

Lot code 260709 with use by date 11/07/2026

The recalled tofu was distributed in 29 states. The report did not indicate which retailers sold the products. See the full list of states:

title: FIRST ON FOX: Texas becomes testing ground for new defense against attacks on America’s water systems
description: Project Watershed 250 pairs AI security tools with Texas water systems to find cyber vulnerabilities before adversaries can exploit them first.
fullText:
FIRST ON FOX: The Trump administration is launching "Project Watershed 250" Monday, Fox News Digital exclusively learned, deploying American artificial intelligence and cybersecurity tools to protect Texas water systems from cyberattacks in a pilot the administration plans to scale nationwide.

"Project Watershed 250 is another example of President Trump putting American families and communities first. President Trump is relentless in his work to secure our critical infrastructure against our most determined adversaries," National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross told Fox News Digital. "President Trump has cemented America's leadership in AI security and innovation and is now bringing those exquisite tools to local communities and utilities in Texas and ultimately, across the nation through the launch of Project Watershed 250 – a scalable cyber water pilot program."

The Trump administration is bringing federal, state and private-sector cyber defenses together in a six-month Texas pilot aimed at finding vulnerabilities in water systems before adversaries can exploit them — while testing whether the model can be expanded across the country.

Investigators Believe Iranian Hackers Are Likely Behind Cyberattack On Minnesota Water Systems: Report

The program will connect Texas water utilities with U.S. cybersecurity companies to test their existing defenses and strengthen vulnerable systems using private-sector cyber and artificial intelligence tools, a White House official told Fox News Digital.

The program will use "red-teaming" to stress-test water utilities' networks, identify weaknesses hackers could exploit and then strengthen those systems with cybersecurity tools, according to a White House official.

Trump Launches Gold Eagle To Hunt Cyber Flaws With Ai

Dragos CEO Robert Lee said that U.S. water infrastructure faces active, documented threats, particularly at small utilities that often lack strong cybersecurity defenses. Lee said Watershed 250 will help get technology, training and support to those vulnerable systems before an attack occurs.

"There is nothing more important to Texans than clean, reliable drinking water. Project Watershed 250 puts federal, state, and private-sector cyber defenses behind our utilities at no cost. The White House, the Texas Cyber Command, and industry now work from the same playbook," said Texas Gov. Greg Abbott.

A White House official, however, said the program is not in response to recent cyberattacks that targeted more than 30 Minnesota water systems, though the incidents underscored vulnerabilities in local infrastructure.

"However, these recent attacks have reiterated the need for this modernization and focus on water systems," said the White House official. "Critical Infrastructure protection has long been a priority for ONCD and President Trump and this effort has been in the works since last year."

Iranian Hackers Attacked Our Water Systems. Here Are 5 Things Our Leaders Need To Do Now

The Environmental Protection Agency and Department of Homeland Security's Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency will serve as federal partners in the effort, while Texas Cyber Command will work alongside the White House with local governments and tech companies such as Microsoft, Reflection AI, Palo Alto Networks and Dragos Inc.

"Few things matter more than the safety of the water Americans drink, and this is a powerful example of how open-weight AI models, built in the U.S. and running on a utility's own systems, can help keep communities safe," said Becky Sosnov, Reflection AI head of corporate affairs.

Anthropic's Mythos Ai Found Over 2,000 Unknown Software Vulnerabilities In Just Seven Weeks Of Testing

China-linked Hackers Infiltrated Us Government Networks Before Fbi Takedown

"Microsoft applauds the administration's leadership in strengthening the cybersecurity of America's water infrastructure and is proud to support the Project Watershed 250 effort in partnership with the Office of the National Cyber Director, the State of Texas, and Texas Cyber Command," said Microsoft US Public Sector president Chris Barry. "By bringing together Microsoft's cybersecurity expertise, threat intelligence, and AI-powered security capabilities, we aim to help water utilities strengthen their resilience against evolving cyber threats and develop scalable approaches that can enhance the security of water systems nationwide."

The push comes as the Trump administration races to build out U.S. data centers to fuel the AI boom, putting more attention on the water and power needed to keep them running.

The pilot program builds on Trump's June executive order on Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security and his Cyber Strategy for America released in March.

title: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
description: As of August, the number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran had reached another million.
fullText:
The elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind.

"It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan.

The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins.

"But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags.

Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran.

They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world.

Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021.

Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt.

The expulsions show no sign of stopping.

The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR.

"In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan.

"We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border.

It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go.

Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all.

"I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry.

"We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says.

"But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police."

Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan.

The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law".

Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden.

The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants".

In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025.

The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel".

The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified".

But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in".

Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children.

Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university?

Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried."

Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified.

"I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house.

"We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside."

He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work.

"I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country.

Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights.

Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN.

But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000.

At the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face.

"There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan."

In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide.

The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition.

"No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive.

But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support".

Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve.

The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule.

But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states.

As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?"

He answers his own question: "Nothing."

We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense.

All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.

Five years after the Taliban swept to power, does the West have any influence?

title: Inside the dangerous US mission that cleared Iran’s mines from Hormuz shipping lanes
description: CENTCOM's Adm. Brad Cooper details how Navy divers, SEALs and air power quietly cleared Iranian sea mines from the Strait of Hormuz shipping lanes.
fullText:
President Donald Trump declared last week that the United States had removed or detonated all mines in international waters in the Strait of Hormuz.

Now, the commander of U.S. Central Command has offered the clearest public account yet of the high-stakes operation behind that declaration: a monthslong effort in which U.S. forces quietly cleared Iranian sea mines from established international shipping lanes used by commercial vessels.

Other threats still stand between the cleared lanes and a return to normal activity in one of the world's most important waterways. The latest maritime guidance still classifies the Strait at a "SEVERE" threat level. Recent attacks have struck tankers near Oman, and oil flows remain far below prewar levels.

"We have successfully cleared sea mines in the Strait's international shipping lanes that were laid months ago by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps," CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said in a video update.

Trump Says Iran's Navy 'Obliterated' As Us Enforces Hormuz Blockade — But Key Threat Remains

"Internationally recognized transit routes in the Strait are free of Iranian sea mines thanks to the incredible work of the U.S. military," Cooper said.

Cooper identified the cleared area as the Strait's Traffic Separation Scheme, the long-standing system of opposing lanes that guides commercial vessels through the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman.

"Our forces meticulously and quietly cleared them of sea mine threats using a combination of Navy divers, Navy SEALs and U.S. air power from the Army, Navy, Air Force and Marine Corps," Cooper said.

The operation was carried out as the Navy was in the middle of a major transition in how it handles mine warfare.

The service had retired its four Bahrain-based mine countermeasure ships the previous year as newer unmanned systems were still being fielded. In April, defense analyst Bryan Clark told Fox News Digital the Navy was at a "nadir" in its mine-sweeping capacity.

At the time, retired Vice Adm. Kevin Donegan, who previously commanded the Navy's 5th Fleet, said newer technology was increasingly being used to locate and neutralize mines, including unmanned systems that map the seabed and identify potential threats before explosive ordnance teams move in.

Cooper's account now shows U.S. forces relied on a broader combination of Navy divers, SEALs and air power to clear the international shipping lanes. CENTCOM has not disclosed the precise role each capability played.

"The circumstances were challenging and dangerous to say the least, but we got the job done," Cooper said. "Bottom line, today, international shipping lanes are open and momentum is building."

Donegan, who was not involved in the current operation, said mine-clearance operations begin with surface and subsurface vessels, including unmanned systems, locating and identifying possible mines. Once mines are identified, autonomous systems, specially trained Navy divers and SEALs can destroy or neutralize them.

Different sections of a waterway can be at different stages of the process at the same time, Donegan said, with forces neutralizing mines in one area while detection and identification continue elsewhere.

Throughout the operation, the Navy continues scanning the waterway to ensure it has not missed any mines, he said.

Donegan said the Navy uses a sophisticated detection model before declaring a waterway clear.

"In simplest terms, they have to conduct enough sweeps of the lanes to drive the probability of detection of mines to virtually 100% in the model," he said.

Donegan said the calculation takes into account factors including the detection systems and their effectiveness, characteristics of the waterway and the type of seabed.

White House Silent On Iran-oman Hormuz Plan Tehran Says Would Ban Us Warships

The Navy has also spent years preparing for such an operation. Donegan said elements of large-scale mine clearance in the Strait have been practiced through recurring NAVCENT mine-countermeasure exercises dating to 2012, along with regular Navy training.

Cooper said U.S. forces have assisted nearly 1,500 commercial vessels through the Strait in recent months by providing coordinated protection. Those ships carried nearly 750 million barrels of crude oil bound for global energy markets, he said.

The CENTCOM commander said the military is pursuing two missions at once: enforcing a naval blockade on Iran and protecting commercial passage through the Strait. He said that since the blockade resumed in mid-July, U.S. forces have turned around 75 vessels attempting to run it and disabled three that failed to comply with directions.

Cooper did not say how many mines U.S. forces found or destroyed.

Axios reported Thursday, citing U.S. officials, that American forces swept more than 200 mine-like objects from the main shipping lane. Of those objects, 11 were actual mines, and only a few had been properly deployed.

The figures illustrate the painstaking identification process Donegan described: Forces must investigate possible threats before determining which objects are actually mines.

CENTCOM has not provided further details on the systems used during the operation or how individual mines were neutralized. A defense official told Fox News Digital that the military would not discuss operational specifics for security reasons.

The broader maritime-security picture has yet to catch up with CENTCOM's declaration.

The latest Joint Maritime Information Center advisory, issued through the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations office on Aug. 25, keeps the Strait of Hormuz at a "SEVERE" threat level and says deliberate hostile action remains highly likely.

The advisory says mine-danger areas remain active and warns of a continued risk from drifting or uncharted mines in and near the Traffic Separation Scheme. It says clearance and mine-surveying operations continue throughout the Strait and that commercial traffic is expected to remain below prewar levels.

The assessment predates Cooper's video update. No public advisory downgrading the threat level or lifting the underlying warnings had been issued as of Friday.

Donegan said the possibility of drifting mines does not disappear entirely after a route has been cleared.

"In the Gulf there is always the danger of drifting mines that are not fixed, that are left over from this conflict or previous ones in the region," Donegan said. "That threat from those in the Gulf has historically been very low, especially due to currents in that area that make it unlikely that drifting mines stay in the lane and contact a commercial vessel."

Commercial crews are also still confronting attacks.

UKMTO reported that tankers near Oman were struck by unknown projectiles on Aug. 24 and Aug. 25, setting off fires that crews later extinguished. All crew members were reported safe in both incidents. The public alerts did not identify the vessels or attribute the strikes.

Oil flows through the Strait stood at about 5 million barrels per day Monday, down from more than 20 million before the war, according to Reuters, which cited provisional Vortexa tracking data.

The recovery remains uneven. Reuters reported Friday that seven commodity vessels transited the Strait on Thursday, down from 17 the day before and below the 10-day average of 15 vessels, based on preliminary shipping data.

Iran and Oman separately announced this week that they were discussing a temporary joint navigation corridor and a joint mine-clearance project. Their statements did not specify whether that work would cover the same Traffic Separation Scheme CENTCOM says U.S. forces have cleared.

Cooper's announcement provides the most detailed official account yet of the operation behind Trump's declaration and marks a significant step toward restoring commercial passage through the Strait.

The U.S. military says the recognized commercial lanes are open and protected. But the latest maritime risk guidance, continued attacks and sharply reduced traffic show that the broader Strait remains dangerous and disrupted.

Original article

title: The House is back in session. Many Republicans hope it won't be for long.
description: If lawmakers can pass a shutdown-averting stopgap, many are hoping to beat an early retreat to the campaign trail.
fullText:
The House is back in session Monday for the first time in five weeks. It's not clear how long members will stick around.

Speaker Mike Johnson is hoping to tick the lone essential item off the chamber's to-do list in lawmakers' first days back: sending a shutdown-averting spending bill to President Donald Trump's desk. Otherwise, the Capitol Hill agenda is devoid of must-pass legislation until later in the year.

Meanwhile, the thin GOP majority has had trouble opening the House floor for debate on any number of legislative priorities, and many Republicans lawmakers are simply eager to get back home ahead of the November midterms rather than endure more headaches in Washington.

Together that has fueled open speculation among members and aides that House leaders will call it quits until mid-November much sooner than the currently scheduled Oct. 1 exit date.

"So many people are having to run back and forth to campaign," Rep. Morgan Griffith (R-Va.) told reporters Thursday. "I think we can get some other things done [beyond the spending stopgap], but the big bills will probably have to wait until after the election."

Another House Republican, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly, was more blunt: "I think we have very little to do." A third member, running for reelection in a competitive district, said in a text message, "I'd be happy to be sent home early!"

The agitation for an early exit is likely to grow louder if Johnson can win approval as planned this week for the Senate-passed government funding bill, which would postpone a possible shutdown from midnight Sept. 30 to Dec. 11. The funding patch also would extend the deadline to reauthorize lapsing surface transportation authorities.

GOP leaders plan to put the bill on the floor Tuesday under a fast-track method requiring a two-thirds majority vote, and there are reasons to believe it will pass without much drama. Trump and key congressional Democrats have endorsed the 10-week punt.

That bipartisan support is expected to overcome Republicans concerns over a Senate-inserted provision backed by the White House to delay the start of an intoxicating hemp product ban, as well as a provision favored by Democrats to temporarily hold up a Trump administration proposal to put political appointees in charge of federal grant approvals.

"I would say that we're going to avoid any kind of shutdown, and we'll be in good shape going into the elections," Rep. Riley Moore of West Virginia, a GOP appropriator, told reporters earlier this month.

Lawmakers have already punted other major deadlines, leaving members eyeing the post-election "lame duck" session for substantive legislating. But there are also lingering questions about whether House Republican leaders can move forward with a partisan agenda in any case.

Rebel factions upset over matters ranging from ethanol fuel regulations to immigration policy votes have frustrated Johnson's attempts all summer to pass procedural measures necessary to bring GOP bills to the floor. Many Republicans believe those dynamics will continue into September, leaving the fast-tracked bills passed under "suspension of the rules" as leaders' only legislative option.

"I don't think many things are going to pass except for suspension bills," said another House Republican granted anonymity to speak candidly about the GOP's expectations for the pre-election session.

While leaders and their top aides acknowledge no current plans to send members home early, a frozen floor could quickly lead them to determine otherwise. At the same time, some Republicans are wary of beating an early retreat after many of them hammered the Senate for leaving town earlier this month without taking up key House-passed bills.

"We need to campaign, but it's not a great look for us to not come into town and work," a fifth House Republican granted anonymity said. The member, representing a safe red district, acknowledged that others in more competitive districts likely feel differently.

"People already think we are on vacation when we're home," the lawmaker added. "What kind of damage does it do if we leave D.C. again?"

Both chambers will be out of session next week following the Labor Day holiday, and many Republican lawmakers are expected to travel to Dallas at the end of that week for the GOP's midterm convention. Republicans are looking to amp up one of their top campaign messages beforehand — that Democrats are left-wing extremists — by forcing a vote this week on a resolution condemning socialism "in all its forms."

The House could also vote this week to censure Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) for inappropriate conduct toward two female staffers following an Ethics Committee recommendation. Edwards, who dropped his bid for reelection two days after the panel issued a lengthy report, attempted to clear his name to his colleagues last week ahead of the expected vote.

House GOP leaders could also put a Senate-passed Russian sanctions bill on the floor before the end of the month, though it is unclear whether it can pass. Many House Democrats — including Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, the party's leader on the Foreign Affairs Committee — believe the bill would give too much authority to Trump.

But with many other House priorities currently in Senate limbo, there could be little incentive for members to hang around to wait to see if the Senate will act once it returns Sept. 14 for a brief three-week session.

House Republicans rushed before their summer recess to adopt a budget blueprint for a fresh party-line spending package, but it's currently stuck across the Capitol amid competing demands from defense hawks, fiscal conservatives and some GOP senators who aren't convinced another such bill is needed at all.

Senate Republicans don't expect the budget measure to be brought to the floor before the election, according to five people granted anonymity to disclose private discussions.

House Republicans appear to be acknowledging that reality. When asked if he was confident the Senate would take up a third reconciliation bill, Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) told reporters this month that "'confident' is probably the wrong word."

Instead, the Senate is expected to focus in September on confirming Trump's nominees and holding a vote on cryptocurrency legislation, as well as trying to advance a bill to overhaul college athletics and the Senate version of the farm bill.

Some House Republicans, including Majority Whip Tom Emmer, have been trying to build public pressure on the Senate to pass the crypto bill known as the Clarity Act for months. But a mid-September vote on that measure is likely to fail. And while negotiations continue over the Senate's college sports bill, a bill on the same topic in the House has stalled out, giving lawmakers little reason to stay to see if a Senate deal comes together.

As for the farm bill, the House passed its version earlier this year largely along party lines, while the Senate version failed to advance in committee earlier this month due to GOP absences and Democratic opposition. Senate Agriculture Chair John Boozman (R-Ark.)said he plans to try again in September.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune is eager to advance the farm bill before the election, but doing so will require Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) to return from a monthslong absence — or Democrats to agree to a deal.

While Republicans are hopeful that McConnell could come back in September, any final agreement on the major agriculture package is expected to wait until after Election Day.

"I think our Democrat colleagues are probably saying we want to wait until after the election to find out what the House of Representatives is going to look like, the Senate is going to look like," Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said at an agricultural conference in South Dakota earlier this month.

Riley Rogerson contributed to this report.

title: How much interest can a $150,000 CD account earn over the next year?
description: Transferring $150,000 into a 1-year CD account could prove to be a safe and lucrative move for savers who act now.
fullText:
If you currently have access to $150,000, maintaining the ability to add and withdraw from it is understandably important right now. With inflation still elevated, the potential for an interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve substantial for when the bank meets again in September and concerns over unemployment growing (not to mention credit card balances rising), sacrificing access to your funds may feel unwise right now. But what if that loss of access and flexibility was brief and temporary? And what if the reward for limiting accessibility was an interest rate of around 4% now?

These are the questions savers contemplating the use of a certificate of deposit (CD) account are contending with right now. By transferring $150,000 into a 1-year CD, for example, savers will be able to protect their principal from market conditions while earning a fixed rate of return for the next 12 months. That's something that variable-rate savings account alternatives can't offer and it's something that investing can't, either. Still, with an early withdrawal penalty looming for savers who can't see the account through to its maturity date and with that penalty being costly on an account of this size, it's important that savers understand the value of the account before getting started.

So, how much interest can a $150,000 CD account actually earn over the next year? That's what we'll break down below.

Learn how much interest you could be earning on your money with a CD account here.

The top 1-year CD account interest rates currently range from 4.20% to 4.30%, though savers may be able to find slightly higher rates by diligently shopping around online. With a $150,000 deposit made now, here's how much interest savers can expect to see once the account matures in one year:

$150,000 1-year CD at 4.20%: $6,300.00 upon account maturity$150,000 1-year CD at 4.25%: $6,375.00 upon account maturity$150,000 1-year CD at 4.30%: $6,450.00 upon account maturity

All three of these rates are up noticeably from where they sat in May, when savers were able to lock in a 4.10% rate (with a return worth $6,150.00). That said, there's no guarantee that they actually will or that banks haven't already taken that possibility into account by preemptively adjusting their rate offers, meaning that there may be no material difference post-Fed meeting. It makes sense, then, to start earning more interest on your money now. With online marketplaces listing rates, lenders, terms and conditions all in one location, you may even be able to get started as soon as today.

title: Dad of third-grade girl in Massachusetts allegedly barged in on by trans student in bathroom calls for action
description: Massachusetts father of third grader alleges transgender student barged in girls stalls and is taking complaint to federal level.
fullText:
The Massachusetts father of a third-grade girl who says his daughter was subjected to a disturbing bathroom incident involving a transgender classmate is not backing down from his fight with the school district.

Luis Rivera, whose daughter attends Rochester Memorial School, has hired attorney Sam Whiting of the Massachusetts Liberty Legal Center after filing a federal Title IX complaint against the Old Rochester Regional School District in May.

A letter filed by Whiting on Rivera's behalf alleges that Rivera's 9-year-old daughter was the victim of sex-based harassment after a transgender female classmate, who was born male, entered her bathroom stall. The letter also alleges that the student had previously watched female students use the bathroom, which Rivera and his attorney argue invaded their privacy and undermined their dignity.

Rivera and his wife, Kerri, along with other parents, have repeatedly contacted Rochester Memorial School Principal Heidi Letendre about the transgender student's use of the girls' bathroom, according to the letter.

Washington Mother Says She Found Adult Male Showering In Women's Locker Room During Children's Swim Meet

"On numerous occasions, during this actual event, we reached out multiple times. And we were told by the principal that no boy is supposed to be in the bathroom. Then somewhere along the line, they changed their story," Rivera told Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital reached out to Letendre for comment.

Rivera said he has attended every school committee meeting since the incident, joining other community members in pushing the district to change its bathroom policy.

He also said he and his wife have decided to remove their daughter from the school for the upcoming school year. His daughter wrote a letter to President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump asking for help with the situation.

"I feel scared to use the girls' bathroom," she wrote.

Washington Mother Pulls Children From School After Pride Lesson Shown In Music Class Without Notice

The dispute centers not only on the alleged incident involving Rivera's daughter but also on the district's interpretation of state and federal anti-discrimination laws, Whiting said.

Massachusetts law prohibits discrimination against students based on protected characteristics, including gender identity, and bars schools from excluding students from "the advantages, privileges and courses of study" they offer.

The Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education also says transgender students should have access to school facilities, including bathrooms, consistent with their gender identity.

For now, however, the Old Rochester Regional School District does not appear to have plans to change its policy regarding transgender students.

In a message to parents, Superintendent Michael Nelson said that, following a Title IX investigation, school staff and district administrators acted in compliance with the law. The decision, he said, was made by an independent decision maker following the complaint brought forward by the Rochester Memorial School parent.

Trump Admin Targets Woke Schools Accused Of Hiding Students' Gender Transitions From Parents

In a written statement, Nelson said the district is bound by the Massachusetts laws.

"Additionally, our schools adhere to the policies and procedures of the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education," he said.

"... We believe that we are bound by law and state education policy and that age-appropriate handling of student matters in a public school setting is best left to the professional educators who know how to do their jobs correctly and effectively," he said.

He also noted that during this process, his educators and administrators have been subject to "innumerable explicit, angry and threatening communications," directly and indirectly through social media.

Fox News Digital reached out directly to Nelson.

Whiting said he and the parents involved are particularly disappointed by the superintendent's response, which he claims downplayed the seriousness of the incident.

According to Whiting, the response amounted to, "Oh, these things just happen between 9-year-olds… sometimes bathroom doors are unlocked and these things happen."

Portland Parent Banned From School Events After Opposing Gender Identity Assignment Files Lawsuit

Whiting said he hopes the U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights will investigate the complaint.

"Ultimately, we hope they will find that the school district is in violation of Title IX and will refer the case to the Department of Justice for enforcement," he said. "School districts who violate Title IX can be at risk of losing their federal funds… We're always hopeful they'll do the right thing, but if they don't, our plan is to try to get this in front of the proper authorities at the federal level."

Rivera said the lack of what he considers meaningful action from the district has left him with no choice but to escalate the matter.

"They haven't taken any remedial action. And so that's why we feel like we have to kind of bring this up to the higher authorities and the federal government," Rivera said. "There's no transparency. There's no accountability. It's just they're running around free, and they're violating these girls' privacy rights, because what happened to my daughter should have never happened if the policies were put into place."

"And I have to deal with her emotional trauma behind this," Rivera added.

title: All you need to know about Transfer Deadline Day
description: Our Ask Me Anything team tell you all you need to know as the summer transfer deadline approaches.
fullText:
It is close to being another record-breaking year of summer spending - and a new high could still be reached on Transfer Deadline Day.

But when are all the deadlines, what rules must clubs comply with, who are some of history's most iconic deadline-day signings - and which moves could still happen?

Here is all you need to know about deadline day - and how you can keep across the action.

Premier League and EFL clubs have until 23:00 BST on Tuesday, 1 September to complete their transfers.

The deadlines for other leagues around the world are:

Ligue 1: Tuesday, 1 September - 18:59

Serie A: Tuesday, 1 September - 19:00

Bundesliga: Tuesday, 1 August - 19:00

La Liga: Tuesday, 1 September - 22:59

Scottish Premiership: Thursday, 3 September - 17:00

Women's Super League: Thursday, 3 September - 23:00

Saudi Pro League: Sunday, 6 September - TBC

Fifa rules state a transfer window cannot last more than 16 weeks in a calendar year.

A deal sheet must be completed by Premier League clubs in the last two hours of a transfer window.

This year, the earliest it can be submitted is 21:00 BST, and must be complete before the 23:00 deadline - giving clubs two hours to finalise required paperwork.

Without all paperwork submitted before 23:00, transfers cannot proceed.

Clubs often leave their transfer dealings to the last minute, and therefore have to submit the form to the Premier League to make sure a move can go ahead.

The deal sheet allows a club to confirm an agreement has been reached and also give themselves more time to submit the remaining documentation.

Players who remain free agents after the closure of the transfer deadline can be signed at any point.

They won't be able to play for their new side immediately - unless there is space in the club's registered 25-man squad - as they have to wait until the next period of registration to come around.

While there is no official deadline that is made public, it is understood the deadline is about a week after the window closes.

A Premier League squad list must not contain more than 25 senior players.

This list is published for each club following the closure of the transfer window.

Of those maximum 25 players, no more than 17 can be registered that are not classed as 'homegrown' talent.

As the 25-player rule only applies to senior players, any squad members under the age of 21 at registration cut-off do not count towards the total tally - meaning clubs can register as many under-21 players as they want.

But clubs must otherwise carefully manage the numbers of senior players on the books, or some will be contracted to a team they cannot play for.

Chelsea have previously faced criticism for an oversized squad that had led to the use of a so-called 'bomb squad' - a practice which has since been outlawed by Fifa.

As always, expect a few late twists and turns when it comes to the final day of the window.

There are however plenty of players whose futures remain up in the air and could be set for a late move.

Manchester City midfielder Jack Grealish looks set to return to Everton on loan, with Toffees winger Iliman Ndiaye heading in the opposite direction for £65m.

Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez has also been linked with a reunion with former boss Enzo Maresca at City. Xabi Alonso's side are set to be looking at Monaco's Lamine Camara to bolster their own midfield.

Elsewhere, Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez is of interest to Arsenal and Barcelona and could leave the Spanish capital prior to the window closing.

Liverpool winger Cody Gakpo has been a target for both Spurs and City, although any exit would be dependent on the Reds securing a replacement - which is increasingly unlikely.

Perhaps the most dramatic signing of the 2025-26 summer transfer window was Alexander Isak's departure from Newcastle United, joining Liverpool on deadline day and breaking the British transfer record in the process.

Some other memorable deadline-day deals over the years include:

Claude Makelele from Real Madrid to Chelsea (2003)

Wayne Rooney from Everton to Manchester United (2004)

Carlos Tevez and Javier Mascherano from Corinthians to West Ham (2006)

Ashley Cole from Arsenal to Chelsea (2006)

Hugo Lloris from Lyon to Tottenham (2012)

Mesut Ozil from Real Madrid to Arsenal (2013)

Cristiano Ronaldo from Juventus to Manchester United (2021)

Cole Palmer from Manchester City to Chelsea (2023)

You can keep tabs on all the action across the BBC as the deadline approaches.

The BBC Sport website and app will have a dedicated live page covering up-to-the-minute Premier League deals, as well as news from the EFL.

BBC Sounds will be keeping across the action on 5 Live and on local radio stations all day across the UK.

Many of the local stations will also have their coverage live streamed so you can watch along - find out all the info here.

This article is the latest from BBC Sport's Ask Me Anything team.

What is the Bundesliga's 50+1 ownership rule?

Why can't Real Madrid play at Anfield in the Champions League league phase?

What happens during a football medical?

title: Woman randomly stabs 2 people in New York City's Times Square, killing 1, then is killed by police
description: A woman randomly stabbed two people in New York City’s Times Square on Monday, killing one woman, and then was fatally shot by police, according to officials.  The shooting happened just before 4:30 p...
fullText:
A woman randomly stabbed two people in New York City's Times Square on Monday, killing one woman, and then was fatally shot by police, according to officials.

The shooting happened just before 4:30 p.m. next to a New York Police Department substation, just outside One Times Square, the building that hosts the city's annual New Year's Eve ball drop celebration. It is one of the most heavily touristed and policed spots in all of New York.

The 49-year-old woman from Queens pulled out two knives from a shopping bag and stabbed a 68-year-old man who had just come out of the subway station and was waiting to cross the street with his wife, striking him in the abdomen, Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said at a news conference.

Seconds later, the woman stabbed a 32-year-old woman also in the abdomen, Tisch said. Both victims were taken to the hospital. The woman died and the man is in stable condition, according to police.

Police didn't say if the victims were tourists visiting the city or residents.

Videos posted on social media show a group of at least 10 officers gathered around the woman, who was holding two large kitchen knives.

Officers tried to convince the woman to drop the knives for several minutes before using a Taser, Tisch said. The woman told them: "I'm not dropping anything, I would rather kill both of you," according to Tisch.

The video shows the Taser not incapacitating her and the woman walking quickly toward the officers while waving the knives in front of her.

Two officers then shot the woman, according to police. In the video posted by bystanders, the woman fell to the ground, where an officer handcuffed her. Officers rolled her onto her back and rendered first aid.

"This was an extraordinarily dangerous situation unfolding in the heart of Times Square, the crossroads of the world," Tisch said.

The woman has a "documented mental health history with the NYPD," which include incidents in 2018 and 2019 but no arrest history with the department, Tisch said. She didn't provide additional details.

Police are investigating. Tisch said there was no evidence suggesting it was a terrorist attack.

The names of the victims have not been released until next of kin are notified, according to police.

"We know that those families' lives have been shattered by what took place today, and we will continue to hold them close as the hours and days and weeks continue from this moment," said Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Both Mamdani and Tisch praised the officers, saying more people could have been hurt or killed if not for their actions.

The NYPD temporarily closed part of 7th Avenue and warned the public to stay away from the area. Police tape cordoned off the area as a large group of law enforcement officers worked nearby.

Violent crime has fallen sharply in New York City so far this year, with homicides down 24% and on pace to potentially hit their lowest level in decades. But this is the second killing this year in Times Square. A man was fatally stabbed in the same area in May.

title: Arsenal agree terms to sign De Almeida from PSG
description: Arsenal agree terms to sign versatile France defender Elisa de Almeida from Paris St-Germain.
fullText:
Arsenal have agreed terms to sign France defender Elisa de Almeida from Paris St-Germain.

Sources in France suggest the fee could be about £550,000 and she is expected to join before Thursday's transfer deadline.

The versatile 28-year-old can play at centre-back - an area where Arsenal need cover at the start of the season because of injuries.

De Almeida has spent five years at PSG, making more than 100 appearances and has experience of competing in the Women's Champions League.

She has spent her entire career in France, representing Paris FC before a spell at Montpellier, prior to joining PSG.

De Almeida has played 52 games for France and was part of Les Bleues' squads at the 2023 Women's World Cup and Euro 2025.

Arsenal are seeking to win a first Women's Super League title since 2019 and have strengthened this summer, with additions including England midfielder Georgia Stanway and Spain full-back Ona Batlle.

Renee Slegers' side start their season at Brighton on Sunday, 6 September (12:00 BST).

title: Wawrinka feels the love on Grand Slam goodbye
description: Three-time major champion Stan Wawrinka is given an emotional send-off at the US Open following the final Grand Slam match of his career.
fullText:
Three-time major champion Stan Wawrinka felt the love at the US Open after being given an emotional send-off following the final Grand Slam match of his career.

The 41-year-old Swiss is retiring at the end of the season and looked close to tears as he received a rapturous reception after a straight-set defeat by Italy's Matteo Berrettini.

Wawrinka, who won the US Open in 2016, was initially overlooked by tournament organisers for a wildcard, but was given a last-minute reprieve following American recipient Patrick Kypson's withdrawal.

The belated decision can be considered well justified given the thousands who packed into the 8,000-capacity Grandstand court at Flushing Meadows.

Wawrinka made heart gestures with his fingers, and put his hand on his heart, at the end of an enjoyable contest to illustrate his appreciation.

With huge cheers already ringing his ears, the former world number three encouraged the crowd to make more noise before knocking balls into the stands as souvenirs of the occasion.

"One of the reasons I played until 41 was to live these moments," said Wawrinka, who also won the Australian Open in 2014 and the French Open in 2015.

"I'm very grateful for this wildcard. It was very important for me to finish here, where I won a Grand Slam 10 years ago. I want to thank you all for all these years."

Djokovic's tearful loss leaves future uncertain

'I felt the love' - how did Alcaraz look on winning singles return?

Wawrinka was only given the news about the wildcard on Wednesday, when he was back in the Swiss mountains having travelled home from New York two days earlier.

Despite the late notice he quickly rearranged a return across the Atlantic in order to play at one of his most loved venues for the final time.

Fans arrived early and waited in long queues to ensure they could witness what they knew could be his Grand Slam goodbye.

It turned out that way as 2021 Wimbledon finalist Berrettini made his veteran opponent pay for not taking his chances.

Wawrinka held set points in each of the first two sets - one in the first and three 

Berrettini led the applause before Wawrinka addressed the crowd and received a photo montage of his US Open triumph from chief executive Craig Tiley.

Afterwards Wawrinka - celebrated for his one-handed backhand and competitive spirit - said he was "super grateful" for the fond farewell.

"It's showed me that I did the right thing all those 20 years by always trying to fight, always showing up, always trying to do my best, and always trying to push myself to the limits," he added.

"This is what for me was the most important thing - what I get from the fans when I play."

title: A newspaper gown and an NBA tribute - Osaka's US Open fashion statement
description: Naomi Osaka has proved she knows how to make a grand entrance at Grand Slams - and has done it again at the US Open.
fullText:
The spectacular jellyfish outfit at the Australian Open. A sparkly Eiffel Tower-inspired golden dress at the French Open. The elegant all-white Japanese kimono at Wimbledon.

Naomi Osaka has proved she knows how to make a grand entrance at the Grand Slams - and her arrival at this year's US Open was always going to turn more heads.

The four-time major champion was draped in a hooded white gown - with cuttings of newspaper headlines about her career highlights sewn in - when she walked out for her first-round match against Russia's Anastasia Zakharova in New York.

Underneath was an all-black basketball-style kit in which Osaka played as she fought her way to a 7-6 (8-6) 7-6 (7-3) win over world number 101 Zakharova.

Afterwards Osaka said the on-court look was inspired by NBA legend Allen Iverson, who is widely credited for introducing a sharper focus on fashion in his sport during the late 1990s and early 2000s.

"He's a trailblazer. I think he's also someone that I look up to a lot, because he's done a lot in fashion, whether it's on purpose or not," said Osaka.

"He's shifted the way that NBA players dress. I also think the whole conversation around clothes in sports and just expressing yourself through style.

"I feel like he's someone that I look up to in that regard."

Osaka's performance on the court in Monday's night session was less stylish, however.

The Japanese 13th seed, who won the Flushing Meadows title in 2018 and 2020, faltered after a strong start and ultimately needed to dig deep to see off Zakharova.

Osaka broke at the first opportunity to take a 2-0 lead in the opener and although she was unable to convert another chance to go 4-0 ahead, still looked comfortable when she moved 5-2 up.

However, Zakharova showed heart as she rallied to take the opener into a tie-break and fought back from another early break down in the second.

Osaka's superb serve came to the fore as she opened up a commanding 5-1 lead in the second tie-break, going on to complete victory just before 00:30 local time and avoiding the need for a deciding set.

The former world number one will face the Czech Republic's Katerina Siniakova in the second round - and promised her fans there will be another sartorial surprise.

"I wanted to play well because I wanted to show you guys some more outfits," she said.

"I love expressing myself through clothes - because I don't like talking too much."

title: Leeds close in on Nice defender Bard
description: Leeds United are closing in on an initial loan move with option for Nice defender Melvin Bard.
fullText:
Leeds United are closing in on an initial loan move for Nice defender Melvin Bard, with the deal containing an option to buy the Frenchman at the end of the season.

The move will see the Yorkshire club pay their French counterparts an initial one million euros, and they can then buy the left-back at the end of the campaign for a further five million euros if they want.

Bard, 25, is travelling to Elland Road on deadline day to complete a medical.

The addition will add depth to the full-back positions with Gabriel Gudmundsson the only current left-sided option available to manager Daniel Farke.

There is also uncertainty around Leeds' attack, with Willy Gnonto in Florence completing a move to Fiorentina.

The initial loan move for the Italian to return to Serie A was contingent on Leeds finding a replacement but they saw a move for Chelsea's Mykhailo Mudryk successfully hijacked by Tottenham.

Bard would be Leeds' sixth senior signing of the summer after goalkeepers James Trafford and Michael Zetterer, defenders Nico Elvedi and Tarik Muharemovic and forward Harry Wilson.

title: I work on AI at Amazon. My biggest career regret is waiting years to build a reputation outside the company.
description: An Amazon employee shares how he built a reputation outside the company — and why the effort can sometimes feel like a second job.
fullText:
Abhinav Bohra's biggest career regret: letting his work stay behind Amazon's walls.

He developed a list of rules for himself to follow as he built greater professional visibility.

Going public opened doors — but added an AI "learning tax" to his nights and weekends.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Abhinav Bohra, a senior applied scientist at Amazon. He's in his 30s and lives in Seattle. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

For most of my career, everything I built lived and died inside Amazon.

I joined Amazon in 2019 as a data scientist and eventually became a senior applied scientist in 2024. My background is in AI recommendation systems, and I work on models that help determine which products shoppers see on Amazon.

While I was building a reputation inside the company, I wasn't building much of one outside it. People in the industry outside Amazon were publishing research papers on the same problems I was solving, and I never joined the conversation.

I eventually realized that without a public record of my work, I was missing opportunities to speak at industry events, serve on conference committees, and build a reputation that could help me if I ever needed to find a new job. When it came to professional opportunities outside Amazon, it felt like I was starting from zero.

The lesson I learned was that internal reputation doesn't travel. My biggest career regret is how long I took to show up outside the company. I'd be a few years further along if I'd realized this sooner.

At first, I was hesitant to publish externally. I treated anything within a mile of my day job as radioactive, which meant I shared nothing publicly. There are processes for publishing company work externally, but they can require documentation and review, and I didn't want to go through that process.

Eventually, I realized I could do external work without using the company's proprietary data or information. The data was proprietary, but my ideas and research were not.

Take a problem I worked on a few years ago: How do you train a good AI model when you have almost no labeled data? Research teams everywhere hit that wall.

I developed some rules for myself. If a problem exists in published research, it's a conversation. If it only exists in our codebase, it's not. Nonpublic data, internal metrics, customers, code, roadmaps, and unreleased products are all off the table. If I'm still unsure, I won't share it.

Business Insider is speaking with tech workers who've found themselves at a corporate crossroads — whether due to a layoff, resignation, job search, or shifting workplace expectations.

Share your story by filling out this form.

It surprised me how much meaningful technical discussion was still possible without revealing anything proprietary.

In 2021, I started taking steps toward sharing more of what I was learning, and I published my first research paper around a year later. Publishing papers opened the door for me to start reviewing other researchers' work and helped me build relationships in the industry.

Eventually, I was able to land some external speaking opportunities. I think having published research and experience reviewing other researchers' work is what made the difference.

Posting on LinkedIn became part of my strategy, too. I shared my research, technical ideas, and conference work. I wasn't trying to become an influencer — I was just trying to build a professional identity that wasn't tied to a single employer.

In recent years, the going-public bet has started to compound in ways I can actually point to rather than just describe.

I've since become a Challenge Co-Chair for ACM RecSys 2026, an international conference focused on recommender systems. I reached out, explaining my background, research, and reviewing record, and said I was interested in serving on the organizing committee.

After the organizers reviewed my background and we spoke on a call, I was appointed. Reaching out got me considered, but the work behind the initial email is what made the opportunity possible.

I've also joined a mentorship program through Johns Hopkins, where I advise early-stage ventures on AI and technical strategy.

Building an external reputation isn't only about having accomplishments to put on my résumé.

I think the work I was doing inside Amazon would have gotten better faster if I'd started engaging with people outside the company earlier.

When you explain your thinking in a paper or on a conference stage, you're writing for people with no context and no reason to be polite. The weak spots in your work show up fast. Strangers make the best reviewers precisely because they owe you nothing.

Over the years, my outside work has made me more confident at Amazon. I think the biggest change was becoming more comfortable contributing an idea before I had every detail perfectly figured out.

AI learning can become an unofficial second job. It's valuable and exciting, but it also blurs the boundary between professional development and personal time. Outside my day job, I spend evenings and weekends researching retrieval and recommendation systems and submitting research papers on the topic.

I enjoy the work, so I don't want to frame it as purely negative. But it does affect work-life balance. There are evenings or weekends when I should probably be disconnected, but I end up spending time on AI because I know the field is moving quickly.

AI creates opportunity, but it also creates a learning tax. For people working close to the field, continuous learning has quietly become part of the job, even when it happens outside the job.

There's value in having a public record of your work if your career ever takes an unexpected turn. Life can be uncertain. There could be layoffs. There could be a difficult job market that makes it hard to find a new job.

You don't want to spend years developing tools, solutions, and expertise, leave a company, and feel like you're starting from scratch because everything you built was proprietary and you can't share it.

My advice to other people working in tech is to make sure you have a profile outside your company that allows someone to understand the value you can bring.

That doesn't mean sharing proprietary information or violating an NDA. There are other ways to build a public record. For me, that means publishing independent research, speaking at industry conferences, reviewing other researchers' work, and becoming involved with organizations related to my field.

title: It's taken me a long time to process Olympic experience - Raygun
description: Australian Olympic breakdancer Rachael Gunn - known as Raygun - tells BBC Sport about the aftermath of her extraordinary experience at the 2024 Olympics.
fullText:
Just hours before representing Australia at the Paris 2024 opening ceremony, Rachael Gunn had a panic attack in the middle of the Olympic village.

Thrust into an environment full of experienced athletes, it dawned on Gunn, whose professional background is as a university lecturer, what she had got herself into.

Known as Raygun when competing, she was about to take part in the breakdancing event - or breaking - which was making its Olympic debut.

"I felt like an imposter," said the 38-year-old breaker, during a new Netflix documentary about her experience at the Games.

She describes how she reacted when she saw someone she recognised from the Olympic team.

"I just could not stop crying... I had a panic attack. 'What am I doing? What have I done? Should I be doing this?'" she said.

Just a few hours later, she was sailing down the River Seine alongside the rest of the Australian cohort, waving to onlookers.

Less than a fortnight after that, her Olympic journey was over. Gunn failed to win any of her three round-robin battles at the Games, but walked away pleased with how she had acquitted herself.

"Finishing my last round, the world champion Nicka [Dominika Banevic] gave me props for my moves, the MC celebrated my stuff and the vibe was just generally good," Gunn told BBC Sport.

What she hadn't anticipated was that one of her performances, in which she debuted some unconventional moves including a sprinkler and a kangaroo hop, had gone viral.

There were memes. There was a sketch on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. Adele referenced the performance in one of her concerts. Chris Hemsworth defended Gunn in an interview with Jimmy Kimmel. At one point in August 2024, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese even felt moved to speak out, praising Gunn for having "a crack".

"It was pretty wild the way I became a topic of conversation in spaces I never thought I would be," said Gunn.

Alongside the teasing, there were more sinister forces brewing, including conspiracy theories about nepotism - for instance that Gunn's husband and trainer, Samuel Free, had been on the selection committee when she qualified to represent her country at the Games, when he hadn't been.

"It was really tough when mine and Sammy's credibility, ethics and motivations were being called into question," Gunn said.

"You could just spend 30 seconds researching and find plenty of sources to debunk these conspiracies, but that's not how people use the internet anymore."

That new-found scrutiny took a toll on Gunn's mental health.

"I felt like my whole life was just kind of crumbling before me.. .and I was just trying to get through the day," she says in the documentary.

In the process of making a film about that time, however, she feels that she's been able to regain some agency.

"It's taken a long time for me to process what happened," Gunn told BBC Sport.

"It's really exciting for me to finally have a voice again."

After it was announced that breaking would be included at Paris 2024, Gunn qualified to represent her country via the Oceania Breaking Championships in Sydney in 2023.

"I've never participated in anything of such high stakes before. It was all international judges, but I was relieved and excited when I qualified. And then the next whirlwind happened," she said.

Quickly, she realised that she would have to start living like an athlete.

Gunn gained a scholarship at the New South Wales Institute of Sport in February 2024, which allowed her to begin a strength and conditioning programme.

"That was great, but also overwhelming because I was training with people who had been doing that stuff since they were kids," she said.

In the midst of her training, the documentary reveals that Gunn's mother suffered three brain aneurisms. Gunn herself began a course of anti-depressants to help with feelings of anxiety.

The film portrays how it began to dawn on her what she had taken on when she entered competitions in the run up to the Games.

"That's when it first starting occurring to me that I was going to be going up against world champs and people who had been winning competitions on big stages for years and years, but I was still going to go out there and do my best," she says in the documentary.

In that context, Gunn decided to play to her own strengths with a creative gamble, developing a routine that paid cheeky homage to her Australian roots.

"I was aware that I was never going to beat my competitors on athleticism," she explained.

"For me, my strength is creativity. With that being one of the [judging] criteria, our thinking was, 'why don't we put all our eggs in that basket and really try and wow them? Maybe we can make a moment.'

"We never, ever expected the impact it might have."

The documentary reveals that head of the Australian Breaking Association, Lowe Napalan, only assisted Gunn's training "a handful" of times in the build-up to the Games, owing to the amount of administrative work taking up his time.

That meant that he only saw Gunn's controversial routine for the first time just before she performed at the Olympics.

"I was there side-stage," Napalan says in the film.

"I had to not have a face of shock."

It was reported in November 2024 that the furore around her Olympic performance had led Gunn to quit breaking.

"I don't know where that came from," Gunn said.

"I wouldn't let what happened take dancing away from me. I love breaking, I'll always break, I'll always be a part of the community."

Her hope is that the release of the upcoming film can help shift the conversation.

"It feels nice to lay it all out there and now be able to look to the future. I'm actually excited about what's to come, which is the first time for a while," she said.

title: Girl who allegedly recorded livestream of Islamic center shooting charged with murder
description: The North Carolina teen was indicted on three counts of first-degree murder.
fullText:
A 17-year-old girl from North Carolina has been indicted on murder charges for allegedly aiding the suspects in the deadly attack on the Islamic Center of San Diego by disseminating a livestream of the May shooting and releasing their writings, officials announced on Monday.

The teen, Sarah Santiago, is being charged as an adult with three counts of first-degree murder and one count of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder, according to an indictment filed Monday in Forsyth County.

A lawyer for Santiago maintained the teen's innocence.

"The discovery in the matter has not been released to me for specific evidentiary comments," the attorney, Alan Doorasamy, told ABC News. "Suffice it to say, this matter is sub judice and at this time I can confirm that my client is innocent of all these charges."

San Diego Islamic Center shooting suspect apparently posted video of attack: Sources

Three men were killed in the May 18 shooting at the Islamic center, which is home to a school where some 140 children were playing in the back at the time gunfire erupted, prosecutors in Forsyth County said.

Two suspects in the attack -- 17-year-old Cain Clark and 18-year-old Caleb Vazquez -- were found dead in a vehicle nearby, authorities said.

"When I looked at this, the facts of this case, the evidence of this case, I realized that what we really had was the purpose and plan of Vazquez and Clark that day was twofold -- number one, it was to kill as many people possible on that day, and secondly, they wanted this -- their carnage and destruction -- recorded, live-streamed and disseminated out," Forsyth County District Attorney Jim O'Neill said at a press briefing on Monday, referring to the two suspects as "domestic terrorists."

Santiago was allegedly communicating with the suspects on Signal leading up to the attack and was among three people who watched the livestream, according to O'Neill. She is also accused of providing a Sonnenrad patch, depicting a neo-Nazi symbol, that Vazquez allegedly wore during the attack, according to the indictment.

"This was not a single-day plan. This had been building up," O'Neill said.

O'Neill said that while Santiago was not in California at the time of the attack, she can be charged with murder in North Carolina because she is accused of aiding and abetting the suspects.

Security guard at Islamic Center of San Diego hailed as a hero

"When someone has credible knowledge that a crime is going to be planned or to be committed, particularly any act of violence, the law requires them to come forward and report it," FBI Charlotte Special Agent in Charge Reid Davis said during the presser. "Failure to do so is not only irresponsible, but it can also be a crime."

The indictment also alleges that Santiago conspired with the two suspects to attack worshippers at a Jewish temple and African-American students at a high school.

The teen, a student in the Winston-Salem Forsyth County school system, was arrested last week ahead of the grand jury indictment, according to O'Neill. He said authorities decided to act because it was close to the start of the school year and holy holidays.

"We looked at the carnage that had occurred in California, and quite frankly, this is a student in the Winston-Salem Forsyth County school system, and the thought of her going back to school, or with the weekend approaching, holy days approaching, we didn't know what she was capable of," O'Neill said. "It was frankly too great a risk to wait until a grand jury could decide."

The investigation is still ongoing, Davis said.

Amin Abdullah, Nadir Awad and Mansour Kaziha were killed in the shooting at the Islamic Center. O'Neill hailed them as heroes.

"The men who died at the mosque that day were men of courage, sacrifice and faith," he said. "They saved countless lives that day."

title: He was dragged 60ft under a bus - now he's fighting for a UFC contract
description: Liam McCracken will compete for a UFC contract on Dana White's Contender Series on Tuesday, three years after he was left fighting for his life when he was hit by a bus.
fullText:
The first thought Liam McCracken can remember having after he woke up was that he was glad to be alive.

On Tuesday, the Briton is set to compete for a UFC contract on Dana White's Contender Series in Las Vegas, but just three years ago he was fighting for his life.

While out on a run near his home in Liverpool, McCracken stepped out into the road without properly checking for oncoming vehicles, and was hit by a bus.

The 25-year-old from Liverpool says he didn't see the bus until the last moment, and was dragged underneath it for 18 metres (60ft) and seven seconds before it stopped.

A couple who saw the incident found McCracken under the bus unconscious and bleeding heavily. They thought he was dead.

If not for passers by on the main road, among them a paramedic with life-saving equipment in their car, McCracken says he would probably have bled to death before an ambulance arrived to take him to hospital.

The accident left McCracken with four fractures in his back, two slipped discs in his neck, three broken ribs, a broken pelvis, a broken nose, a ruptured anterior cruciate knee ligament, a torn meniscus and multiple other wounds.

For a long time he worried he might never walk or compete again - but remarkably, he will fight Mexican lightweight Silvestre Sanchez on Tuesday.

"For the first few days I wasn't caring about anything else other than the fact that I was alive," McCracken tells BBC Sport.

"I have a little daughter and apparently the people who found me said that was the first thing I kept speaking about when I regained consciousness.

"I kept asking about my little girl while I was on the floor getting seen by people. The main thing was I was glad to be alive."

McCracken says the incident and recovery which followed were some of the most difficult moments of his life but he tells the story in good humour.

"My girl had just turned one. One of the funniest things is she wasn't walking at the time and literally a day or two after it happened she started walking. I stopped being able to walk while she'd just learned to walk," says McCracken.

McCracken was not only unconscious but was being burned by the engine of the bus - but the driver could not turn the ignition off because the suspension would have dropped, with the vehicle potentially crushing him.

A pedestrian had to help the driver guide the bus away from McCracken before anyone could tend to him.

"A woman was with me holding my hand on the floor and then loads of people started coming over," said McCracken.

"They came over and saw to me straight away which basically saved my life because I was losing a lot of blood. I had to get multiple blood transfusions."

At the time McCracken had won five of his six fights as a professional and was being touted as a future UFC star, but he had a long road ahead of him if he was to make his dream a reality.

McCracken says there were serious doubts whether he would fight again because doctors said he might need a metal rod in his back, which would have ended his career.

However, after multiple X-rays, it was determined he would not need it.

"It was a long road and very up and down and if things along the way went a little different, I wouldn't be back fighting," he said.

"It was the longest six months of my life and I finally started to get somewhere when I had to have knee surgery, which is a massive surgery.

"So I had to basically start all over again. That was one of the hardest parts."

After multiple operations followed by hours of physio and training, McCracken eventually returned to action almost two years after the accident.

"It was very up and down and I did some stupid stuff like trying to jump back into training when I wasn't ready to," said McCracken.

"Obviously it was stupid - but the mentality I had was I wasn't going to let it stop me, and that's what's allowed me to get back in a way."

McCracken won via a rear-naked choke againstg Brazil's Jhon Bryan on his return, but says his performance was not up to his usual standard because he was not fully focused on his opponent.

"It was like I was in a film. I was looking around thinking 'how is this happening'?" said McCracken.

"I didn't ever think it was going to happen. It felt like I was having an out of body experience."

McCracken says the accident has "made him a lot more grateful for life" and the phrase "you could get hit by a bus tomorrow" has taken on a whole new meaning for him.

"When it actually happens to you it's real. I could go from this interview now and cross the road and my life could be over, so it makes you much more grateful," said McCracken.

"You're grateful for just being able to walk because I know what it's like to have your dignity stripped from you."

McCracken started MMA as a hobby as a youngster but with two children now, he sees the sport as a way to provide "financial freedom" and to give his family a life that he "wouldn't be able to do working a normal job".

A statement win on the Contender Series would provide a large step towards achieving his goal, as well as completing a remarkable recovery from a near-death experience.

"I feel really good and after everything I've been through I feel like I'm ready, mentally, for anything in life," said McCracken.

"The fight doesn't feel too big. I feel like I would have had impostor syndrome a couple of years ago, whereas now it feels right and I'm ready for it."
