title: The Latest: SCOTUS allows Trump’s White House ballroom construction to continue
description: A divided Supreme Court on Monday allowed the White House to continue construction on a $400 million ballroom project as lawsuits play out.  Venezuelans are expressing outrage and the oil industry is ...
fullText:
A divided Supreme Court on Monday allowed the White House to continue construction on a $400 million ballroom project as lawsuits play out. The decision replaces a temporary order from Chief Justice John Roberts previously issued hours before a lower-court decision halting the work would have gone into effect. The lawsuit will return to lower courts, but documents say that key portions of the project could be complete within months — a quick timeline compared with a typical legal case.

Venezuelans are expressing outrage and the oil industry is waiting for details on President Donald Trump's announcement that Venezuela 's acting president has agreed to give an unnamed U.S. company control of vast amounts of the South American country's untapped oil reserves, at cost. Trump called it "THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!" but critics say U.S. consumers won't benefit for many years.

Global crude prices are rising again after renewed warfare between the United States and Iran, the first significant military action in a month. The global energy supply shock has for the first time kept average prices Americans pay at the pump above $4 throughout August, according to the AAA.

Trump says he wants Congress to create federal tax incentives to promote making television and movies in the United States.

Trump in a social media post said that the idea of a tax incentive has been urged by actor Jon Voight and others in the industry. The president says that too much of the industry's work has shifted to Canada and elsewhere.

Trump made the case for tax incentives without offering details on how it would work, but argued that the "amount of money spent on Tax Incentives will be made up tenfold by the money pouring into the Treasury's coffers."

"Meetings are being set up with the Leaders of both Parties in order to get this done," Trump added. "It should be Bipartisan, especially since so much money is being lost in California, and other largely Blue States."

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is stepping down after 18 months on the job, the White House said Monday, in the latest departure of a top military leader during the Trump administration.

No reason was given for the departure of Driscoll, who is a friend of Vice President JD Vance, but tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have been widely reported. It marks the latest in a series of shakeups of top military leadership, with the Army especially seeing major upheaval.

"Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump's agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more," White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement.

The Supreme Court is being asked to intervene in a dispute over whether a proof-of-citizenship voting measure can appear on the ballot in Michigan.

Supporters filed an emergency appeal Monday after state officials declined to certify the proposal for the ballot following a contentious signature validation process.

Backers turned in more than 700,000 signatures in March.

If passed, the initiative would require the secretary of state to review driver's license records and other data to determine if registered voters are citizens.

Voters who are flagged would be removed from the voter rolls if they cannot provide proof of citizenship.

The Michigan initiative comes as Republicans in several states move forward with similar measures even as the U.S. Senate remains deadlocked over Trump's call for strict citizenship voting requirements.

Brazilian and American officials restarted talks on Monday over U.S. tariffs of up to 37.5% on Brazilian exports. The meeting between Brazilian ministers and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer followed discussions between Trump and Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silv.

Brazil's government said in a statement it is open to dialogue, though it considers the U.S. imposed tariffs incompatible with trade rules, highlighting a $424 billion U.S. trade surplus with Brazil over 15 years.

description: A U.S. judge said the former parent of Silicon Valley Bank cannot pursue a $1.71 billion claim against the FDIC stemming from the bank's March 2023 collapse, one
fullText:
Aug 31 (Reuters) - A U.S. judge said the former parent of Silicon Valley Bank cannot pursue a $1.71 billion claim against the FDIC stemming from ‌the bank's March 2023 collapse, one of the largest U.S. bank failures.

In a ‌206-page decision on Friday, U.S. District Judge Beth Labson Freeman in San Jose, California, held that a trust that took ​over the parent's claims was responsible for former executives' ill-fated decisions to try boosting profit by investing heavily in long-term government bonds and mortgage-backed securities.

What consequences did executives face for their decisions?

Why did Silicon Valley Bank collapse in March 2023?

What was the $1.71 billion claim against the FDIC?

How did rising interest rates impact the bank's portfolio?

Silicon Valley Bank collapsed after rising interest rates caused at least $4.52 billion of losses in the bank's investment portfolio, sparking a bank run that ‌disrupted many technology startups whose deposits ⁠it held.

Most of the bank's deposits were uninsured. The bank's demise presaged the collapses of two other large lenders in 2023, Signature Bank and ⁠First Republic Bank.

Silicon Valley Bank's holding company has been succeeded by SVB Financial Trust. Lawyers for the trust did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Monday. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corp ​and ​its lawyers did not immediately respond to similar requests.

Freeman said the bank's ‌chief financial officer, treasurer and others acted negligently by taking excessive interest rate and liquidity risks, with encouragement from the board of directors.

She rejected the trust's arguments that it was protected because directors exercised their business judgment in authorizing the investments, and the losses occurred only because the FDIC sold the securities at a loss.

"The holding company chose to run the bank ‌through holding company officers in accordance with the ​global, enterprise-wide policies, limits, and metrics that the holding company ​established," Freeman wrote. "Having made this choice, it ​must live with the consequences."

Freeman ruled after a 12-day, non-jury trial.

Silicon Valley ‌Bank had about $209 billion of assets before ​it failed.

The FDIC is ​also suing 17 of the bank's former executives and directors, including onetime Chief Executive Gregory Becker, to recover billions of dollars for alleged gross negligence and breaches of ​fiduciary duty.

Washington Mutual is the ‌largest traditional U.S. bank or thrift by assets to fail, collapsing in 2008. ​First Republic, Silicon Valley Bank and Signature rank second, third and fourth.

title: Republicans ask Supreme Court to let them air TV ads for less
description: Republican campaign groups – supported by the Trump administration – asked the Supreme Court on Monday to let them purchase television advertising at discounted rates
fullText:
Republican campaign groups – supported by the Trump administration – asked the Supreme Court on Monday to let them purchase television advertising at discounted rates, handing the nation's highest court another emergency appeal that could influence the outcome of this year's midterm elections.

The quick-turn appeal follows a series of high-profile decisions from the 6-3 conservative court that have largely benefited Republicans. A separate case dealing with President Donald Trump's controversial executive order on mail ballots is also expected to rocket back to the justices in the coming days.

The latest case involves television advertising, often the most expensive part of a congressional campaign. Candidates benefit from a federal law that requires broadcasters to charge them deeply discounted ad rates. Earlier this year, the Federal Communications Commission said that political parties and other entities are also entitled to the lower rates.

The FCC decision was widely seen as benefiting the Republican Party, which generally tends to raise more money through the party committees. Democrats, by contrast, generally raise more money directly through their candidates.

The House and Senate Republican party committees told the Supreme Court on Monday that they had "budgeted tens of millions of dollars in ad buys under these rules." But, because of the appeals court decision, "broadcast stations are already rescinding those rates."

The Republican committees argued in their filing that federal courts lack jurisdiction to decide the case because the FCC's "interpretive guidance" was "neither agency action, nor final."

They have asked the court to act by Friday.

The Trump administration, which is eager to keep Republican control of Congress, submitted a brief shortly after the appeal was filed supporting the GOP groups. The Justice Department argued that the FCC guidance doesn't harm the Democratic candidates who sued because the rule is applied universally to all candidates and groups.

"The notice does not grant favored treatment to one side or the other; instead, the notice's interpretation offers the same benefit to all sides, including the challengers themselves and the committees and parties supporting them," Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration's top appellate attorney, told the Supreme Court.

A divided three-judge panel of the 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled last week that federal law provides the lower rate only for candidates.

"The term 'candidate' means 'candidate,'" wrote US Circuit Judge Robert King, who was appointed to the bench by President Bill Clinton.

US Circuit Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III, a long-serving conservative appointed by President Ronald Reagan, dissented. He argued that collaboration between candidates and parties has a rich tradition in the United States and described the 4th Circuit's decision as an "assault" on that tradition.

"Congress cannot dangle lower rates for some candidate speech as a means of penalizing other candidate speech," he wrote.

Four Democratic candidates sued over the FCC's decision: Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan, former Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio, Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, and former Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina. The campaign arm for House and Senate Republicans intervened to defend the FCC's decision.

The Supreme Court in late June rolled back longstanding limits on how much political parties may coordinate with federal candidates. Since the 1970s, political party committees were capped at how much money they may spend in coordination with a campaign. That pushed a flood of campaign money toward super PACs, which have no spending limits, but are unable to run their advertising and other messages past candidates they want to help.

In a 6-3 decision decided along ideological lines, the court ruled that those caps violated the First Amendment. That decision was a victory for Republicans principally because of the ad rate issue.

The Supreme Court is likely to act on the emergency appeal in coming weeks.

fullText:
After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

Konstantinos Tzolakis (Hull City): Again, another massive performance, another clean sheet. Hull have taken everyone by surprise, but it's because of that defensive shape and defensive organisation, and obviously, he is at the heart of that as well.

Semi Ajayi (Hull City): Coming up with Hull is the only way he was going to ever play in the Premier League. He has been doing the rounds in the Championship for years. A real good solid pro. He has taken this opportunity and he's been an absolute beast, so fair play to him.

Nordi Mukiele (Sunderland): He was great last season, a real, real powerful centre-half. Again, a top performance from him. Fulham had no shots on target - he was a massive part of that.

James Tarkowski (Everton): It was a captain's performance for Everton. Just one of those guys that you want in your team. No-one ever respects him, no-one ever rates him, but when you play against him and when he's in your team, he's a real bloke. Proper captain, proper leader of men, and kept going right to the end. And ultimately, even though the two Bournemouth defenders decided to mark themselves, he was the one who got the goal.

James McAtee (Nottingham Forest): He absolutely ran the game at Anfield from start to finish. Getting on the ball in the pockets, half-turn, playing forward. He was the reason they were any good, and he's very, very good, but won't be spoken about in the same breath as the goalscorers.

Bruno Fernandes (Manchester United): There's not much more to say. Captain Fantastic, three goals, an assist, and nearly scored from the halfway line. Where would Manchester United be without him? Relegated is the answer.

Rayan Cherki (Manchester City): My favourite player in world football to watch. Amazing the way he's gifted with the ball, the way he manipulates the ball, and also the way he's able to think for himself. And I just like the fact he's carefree. He just wants to play football, so that's great.

Anthony Elanga (Newcastle): Back-to-back weeks, another great goal, another great performance. Just looks like he's had another lease of life under this manager. And I wonder whether we're going to see the Elanga that we saw at Nottingham Forest, just terrorising defences with that pace. But also, before he even gets there, they're just worried about what he can do.

Yoane Wissa (Newcastle): I had to shoehorn him in because ultimately he's been great through the middle, but the two strikers have actually scored more and played better than him. But Wissa's a massive part of why Newcastle have done well, although he's not being talked about enough in terms of the application that he puts in. So much so, that Woltemade could be sold. That's how much of a good job Wissa has done.

Joao Pedro (Chelsea): He has had an unbelievable start to the season. I think under Xabi Alonso, and with Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers behind him, he's going to have an unbelievable season. But also the fact that he wasn't even picked for the World Cup. Brazil manager Carlo Ancelotti was there, and Joao Pedro looks like he has a point to prove.

Erling Haaland (Manchester City): The beast, the Viking, the new haircut. Two goals, comfortable. Just looks like actually playing football is too easy for him. He looks like scoring goals is just becoming a bit boring and he's probably trying to think of ways to do it better.

title: Arteta joins elite 250 club - but where does he rank?
description: At full-time in Arsenal's 1-0 win at Aston Villa, the travelling supporters sang about how their team will win the league again with Mikel Arteta in charge.
fullText:
When thinking of the greatest managers of the Premier League era, Arsene Wenger, Sir Alex Ferguson and Pep Guardiola are names that belong high on the list.

They are three of the rare breed to have managed 250 games with a single Premier League club, and Mikel Arteta is now the 10th member of that elite group.

Monday's 1-0 win over Aston Villa was the 250th top-flight game in charge for Arteta with the Gunners, and his champions delivered a trademark performance.

At full-time at Villa Park, the travelling supporters sang about how they are going to win the league again with Arteta in charge.

With Arsenal coming into this season as trophy holders, and with transition affecting rivals Liverpool, Manchester City, Chelsea and Manchester United, it is hard to see how the fans' partisan prediction is going to be proved wrong.

Arsenal conceded the fewest goals in the league last season as they won the title for the first time in 22 years.

And during Arteta's nearly seven years in charge, the Gunners have become renowned for their defensive excellence.

Against Aston Villa they showed it again, without allowing a shot on target against them as Bukayo Saka's second-half goal secured victory.

The latest win not only puts Arteta in the 250 club. He also has the fourth-best win percentage among those bosses, with only Guardiola, Ferguson and Jurgen Klopp ahead of him.

Arteta is the longest-serving current Premier League manager and with his longevity has come an Arsenal identity.

Arsenal have become renowned for being difficult to break down and new players repeatedly say that they are impressed and sometimes overwhelmed by the level of detail coming from Arteta.

This is the fifth season in a row where Arsenal have won their first two Premier League matches and they again have a solid platform to build another title challenge.

The Gunners have only faced three shots on target in their first two Premier League games. Villa drew a blank in that regard.

During their title triumph last season, the Gunners did not allow their opponents a shot on target in six league matches, the joint-most of any side in a campaign on record since the 2003-04 season.

Goalkeeper David Raya has won the the Golden Glove award for the most clean sheets in each of the past three seasons, while William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhaes have been voted in the PFA team of the year for the past three seasons too.

Since the start of March, the Gunners have kept eight Premier League clean sheets – three more than any other side and the only side in Europe's big-five leagues to have kept more are Juventus with nine.

"It's how they defend as a team and how they attack as a team," Arsenal's record goalscorer Thierry Henry told Sky Sports after the game.

"One thing is sure with Arsenal - everybody needs to run. You don't have any passengers in that team. This is how you win a title. You can see they are so good at it."

The Gunners spent £250m last summer bringing in eight players as they won the title and have already spent about £200m this year, turning Piero Hincapie's loan deal into a permanent one (£34.5m), signing Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle United (£75m), Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge (£34m) and bringing in Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa (£55m).

"That is what we need," Arteta said, speaking to Sky Sports when asked about his squad depth.

"The players that come in make the difference. All of them contributed to create more dominance and more momentum.

"The level of focus and the way they want to contribute to the team, that is going to be decisive in the season."

Arsenal's strength in depth cannot be understated, but one area they may still look to strengthen in is the forward area.

The Gunners have been on the hunt for an elite forward to lift their attack and still could be active on Tuesday's deadline day.

They had an unsuccessful pursuit of Real Madrid winger Vinicius Jr, while they also have a long-standing interest in Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez.

"We are trying to improve the squad and until tomorrow night we will try to do it," Arteta said.

"I have been disconnected from the world for the last 24 hours because my energy has to be on the match, but I will get back on it now."

When pushed about a deal for Alvarez, Arteta said: "I don't know, that's for the people upstairs."

Whatever happens in Arsenal's search, they are going to be hard to keep off the top of the table with Arteta at the helm.

title: China warns of 'consequences' over Taiwan presence at Pacific leaders meeting
description: China said it had serious concerns about Taiwan's presence at the annual Pacific Islands Forum in Palau, warning of "consequences"
fullText:
SYDNEY/WELLINGTON, Sept 1 (Reuters) - China said it had serious concerns about Taiwan's presence at the annual Pacific Islands Forum in Palau, warning of "consequences" after the democratically ruled island ‌attended the group's opening ceremony on Monday.

China views Taiwan as its own territory, and China-Taiwan tensions ‌have featured prominently at the meeting, which is intended to demonstrate regional unity.

"There will always be consequences," Qian Bo, China's special envoy for Pacific ​island affairs, said of Taiwan attending the event. "It's not a threat," he said without specifying what the consequences would be.

"This is objected to by all, so this should not have happened. We think it's very inappropriate to do so," he told reporters on Monday after an opening ceremony in Palau, an archipelago of over 500 islands that has maintained diplomatic ties ‌with Taiwan.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said "the ⁠Pacific Islands Forum determines what happens here, not any other country," when asked by reporters about the Chinese envoy's remarks.

"This is primarily a gathering of the Pacific family ... and I ⁠look forward to the engagement," Albanese said on Tuesday.

New Zealand's Foreign Minister, Winston Peters, echoed this sentiment, saying the group does not take instructions from countries outside of it.

"Taiwan is honoured to serve as a partner in the Pacific, continuing to stand ​with ​everyone and work together to make the Pacific more prosperous ​and peaceful," Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung said on ‌Monday.

Lin Chia-lung was invited for meetings and side events held alongside the forum. Taiwan is not a formal dialogue partner of the forum like China, but a development partner. The U.S., EU, Britain, Canada, India and Japan are also among the 21 dialogue partners of the forum.

China has gradually whittled away the number of Pacific Island countries with formal ties to Taipei, with only three remaining — Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands.

The leaders of Fiji, Vanuatu, Samoa, Solomon ‌Islands and Kiribati did not attend the gathering of the 18-member ​group that counts Australia, New Zealand and Pacific island nations as ​members. Ministers are attending in their place.

Though China ​is Australia's largest trading partner, Canberra remains wary of Beijing's expanding influence in the Pacific ‌and has stepped up security and development ties with ​island nations to deter any ​permanent Chinese military presence in the region.

Australia, New Zealand and the United States have long considered the South Pacific to fall within their sphere of influence.

In the latest sign of that effort, New Zealand and ​the U.S., in a joint statement released ‌on Tuesday during the summit, said they would jointly fund a major upgrade of a World ​War Two port on a Cook Islands' atoll.

title: Billions in US aid to Ukraine under microscope as corruption rocks Zelenskyy’s inner circle
description: Over 24 federal agencies oversee billions in U.S. defense aid to Ukraine as Zelenskyy dismisses officials amid widening anti-corruption probes, expert says.
fullText:
Washington is relying on extensive safeguards and dozens of oversight agencies to scrutinize and protect billions of dollars in U.S. aid to Ukraine amid the country's continuing struggle with corruption, a regional security expert said Sunday.

The oversight comes as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's inner circle faces renewed political pressure from widening investigations, with several senior officials and aides resigning, being dismissed or facing investigations since 2025.

Zelenskyy dismissed Iryna Mudra, a deputy head of the presidential office, on Aug. 19 as anti-corruption investigators pursued a money-laundering case involving another deputy head of the office.

Investigators have not named Mudra as a suspect, The Associated Press reported.

Zelenskyy Says Putin 'Lost The Initiative' As Ukraine's Tech Industry Reshapes The War

"Of course, in all of the former Soviet Union countries, there is significant corruption," former Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Carrie Filipetti, now executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition, told Fox News Digital.

"A lot more work needs to be done. But we know, at least on the U.S. side, as we're providing support for their military, we have a lot of mechanisms," she said before explaining how dozens of agencies are working on oversight of U.S. aid to Ukraine.

The U.S. committed $67.8 billion in defense articles and services to Ukraine from February 2022 through March 2026 through the Presidential Drawdown Authority, the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative and Foreign Military Financing, congressional reports show.

That support is part of a broader U.S. response to the war.

About $195 billion has been appropriated for Operation Atlantic Resolve, including funds to replenish U.S. weapons stocks, support U.S. military operations in Europe and provide economic, development and humanitarian assistance, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.

As Trump's Nato Gamble Pays Off, Envoy Names Allies He's Still Watching

"Over 24 federal agencies are involved in oversight," Filipetti said. "To make certain that there are no consequences to the U.S. taxpayer, to our equipment in terms of the corruption issue, U.S. contributions are very much protected."

In recent months, however, senior Ukrainian officials have resigned, been dismissed or faced scrutiny by the country's independent anti-corruption bodies, including Nabu.

Those developments include Andriy Yermak's Nov. 28, 2025, resignation after investigators searched his premises and Mudra's Aug. 19 dismissal during a money-laundering probe.

Former Deputy Prime Minister Olha Stefanishyna was dismissed by Zelenskyy as Ukraine's ambassador to the U.S. on Aug. 3, two days before a suspicion notice was served against her, according to the Kyiv Post.

He also fired Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov on July 15 in a broader reshuffle over internal wartime disagreements which sparked protests across the nation.

Zelenskyy Pressures Us And Europe For More 'Air Defense' Assistance Amid Ongoing War With Russia

In interviews after he left government, Fedorov also complained about what he described as ingrained corruption and patronage networks, Reuters reported.

"We've seen that Zelenskyy is taking really seriously the criticisms of corruption, and every time there is an allegation, he moves very swiftly to remove those individuals from the government," Filipetti said.

"And the fact that there are these independent bodies is, I think, really important. They're listening to them. They're making sure that they're trying to root it out as much as humanly possible."

The Two Most Important American Weapons Systems Nato Is Eager To Have

Zelenskyy has pushed back on suggestions that the investigations implicate him personally.

"The heads of anti-corruption agencies have zero questions for me," Zelenskyy said in remarks published Aug. 23 regarding the investigations. "They understand perfectly well that I am not involved in anything like that."

A February 2024 USAID inspector general review also found that the agency did not independently verify some Ukrainian health workers' salary claims before reimbursement, though Filipetti said U.S. economic aid is now reimbursed only after verification.

"A lot of what the United States has been providing, we're making sure that everything is through a reimbursement mechanism," Filipetti said.

Top Ukrainian Officials In Zelenskyy Government Submit Resignations Amid $100 Million Corruption Scandal

She said U.S. aid has not been tied to the money-laundering allegations and remains protected as Ukraine works to combat corruption.

The scrutiny also comes as Kyiv faces shortages of Patriot interceptors amid intensified Russian strikes and a need for air defense interceptors.

Zelenskyy said he wants to secure 300 additional interceptors for the coming winter, while Ukraine's air force has requested 360.

"One of the most urgent needs that the Ukrainians have right now is interceptor missiles," Filipetti said. "This is why this idea of sending Patriot capabilities and allowing them to produce them on the ground in Ukraine has become so important to Zelenskyy."

Russia's Gas Gamble Backfires As Trump's Energy Vision Reshapes Europe

President Donald Trump has expressed reluctance to further deplete U.S. missile inventories, saying the United States also needs the weapons, while pressing European allies to shoulder more of Ukraine's defense burden.

"We want missiles too," Trump said Aug. 6 when asked about Zelenskyy's requests for long-range missiles and Patriot systems. "Biden gave him so much, Biden gave $300 billion worth of ammunition."

Filipetti also said Ukraine's anti-corruption efforts remain an important consideration for its NATO aspirations.

"I think every country has been really adamant that the Ukrainians move forward in their anti-corruption mechanisms," Filipetti said.

"Obviously, if Ukraine ever wants to be a formal member of NATO, that's something that they will need to prove and demonstrate."

title: Max Miller and ex-girlfriend Stephanie Grisham ordered to remove social media posts in GOP lawmaker’s latest court fight
description: GOP Rep. Max Miller spent Monday morning not on the campaign trail, but Zooming into an Ohio courtroom in a dispute with ex-girlfriend and former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham, the sec...
fullText:
GOP Rep. Max Miller spent Monday morning not on the campaign trail, but Zooming into an Ohio courtroom in a dispute with ex-girlfriend and former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham, the second time the embattled congressman has been forced to appear in county court in less than a week.

As House lawmakers return to Washington for a sprint ahead of the midterms, Miller appeared from DC via Zoom to address whether he violated a 2023 settlement agreement with Grisham. That agreement came after Grisham alleged Miller abused her, he denied the allegation and then sued her for defamation. As part of their deal, Grisham and Miller were barred from disparaging each other publicly.

It's the latest legal battle facing Miller as he runs for re-election in a district Trump won in 2024 by more than 10 points but Republicans now fear will be competitive over his legal and personal issues. The congressman has faced calls from some Senate Republicans to step down, but Speaker Mike Johnson told CNN on Monday that he supports Miller's reelection bid, calling him "a great member of Congress."

Miller is also locked in a bitter custody battle with his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, the daughter of GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno. She has alleged that Miller abused her, including holding a gun to her when their daughter was an infant. Miller has denied the allegations. Miller came to court in person in that custody case last week.

Zooming in to the wood-paneled courtroom Monday, Miller faced questions over his social media habits, recent media interviews and whether he called Grisham a liar after the two of them entered into the 2023 settlement agreement.

After hours of testimony, the judge issued preliminary injunctions against Miller and Grisham and ordered both parties to take down numerous social media posts that could be construed as disparaging the other.

Miller was pressed on a post from his X account on May 7 describing audio of Emily Moreno discussing allegations Grisham made against the congressman. Along with the audio, the post read, "here is a recording from 2024. In it, Ms. Emily Moreno admits 1.) everything alleged by Stephanie Grisham was fabricated."

Grisham told the court the post had caused damage to her reputation and shattered the peace she sought in the aftermath of the 2023 settlement agreement.

"When a sitting member of Congress calls you a liar, that is a pretty big deal in political circles," Grisham testified.

Miller argued he never posted any of the material himself and does not have social media on his cell phone. He also argued that his job makes him too busy to be concerned with constant updates to social media, and blamed the May 7 posts on staffers.

"I didn't instruct them to do this, period. They just did it," Miller said of the posts.  "You are making it seem like Twitter is 90 percent of a congressman's job."

The congressman was also pressed on two separate news interviews he did, including one with CNN's Jake Tapper.

In that interview, Tapper asked Miller specifically about Grisham and Moreno's allegations and whether people were supposed to believe they were lying. Miller told Tapper "yes," which Grisham's lawyers argued was a breach of the agreement.

At another point in the interview, Miller told Tapper that he could not get into details about the Grisham allegations because of a settlement agreement that had been reached.

Miller argued in court Monday that he was merely defending himself in the interviews, and that Grisham disparaged him first in the court of public opinion. He also argued that public accusations can cause reputational harm even if they are not true.

"We live in a society where the court of public opinion matters more than facts, at least in my world," he told the court.

The congressman's lawyer Adam Brown alleged that Grisham posted on April 22 about Miller, although she did not do so by name. Brown pointed to a post in which Grisham wrote on X on April 22, "Today I feel broken over what so many men with money and power get away with over & over & over," with a broken heart emoji. "Almost worse is those of you who know & do/say nothing as it happens time & again."

April 22 was the same day that TMZ published a story about Miller with the headline "police investigate child neglect claims in nasty custody battle."

Grisham testified the post was not about Miller, but was a reference to several developments in the ongoing controversy around convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, which has generated regular news headlines.

During her testimony, Grisham also argued that Miller's statements about her had an impact on her personal and professional life, that she suffered from worsening anxiety and often turned down opportunities to participate in television appearances out of fear that she may be asked about Miller, an issue she said she couldn't address given the settlement agreement.

"It has been horrible," she said.

CNN's Alison Main, Manu Raju and Casey Riddle contributed

title: DSA leader's working-class image takes hit as public records pile up contradictions
description: Gustavo Gordillo, NYC Democratic Socialists of America co-chair, faces scrutiny over claims about his immigrant parents, union status and housing.
fullText:
The contradictions are piling up around New York City Democratic Socialists of America co-chair Gustavo Gordillo, whose claims about his working-class credentials — from being a "union electrician" to his housing and family story — have increasingly collided with public records and other evidence.

Gordillo has repeatedly invoked his family's immigrant success story while explaining his support for socialism.

"My parents came here, they had nothing," Gordillo told the New York Times in a profile piece earlier this month. "Their first jobs were in fast food and cleaning houses. They built success in this country. And they're absolutely the exception."

According to Gordillo, he advances the cause of socialism because he believes it can "build a world" where his parents' success story is "not exceptional."

Luxury Travel, Shopping, Six-figure Income: Battleground Dems Ripped For 'Phony' Working-class Narrative

A 2021 obituary for Gordillo's paternal grandfather, however, raises questions about the family history behind that account, the New York Post reported Saturday.

Manuel Gordillo, Gordillo's grandfather, emigrated from Peru to the United States to practice medicine in 1958. After settling in the United States, Manuel met his future wife in St. Louis, and the couple later had Gordillo's father, Gustavo, per the obituary.

The obituary also notes that Gordillo's grandfather built a successful life as a psychiatrist in Ohio, at one point serving as the president of the Ohio Psychiatric Association, casting doubt on the socialist's claim that his parents grew up in poverty.

"My dad, his first job in the United States was working at Wendy's, my mom's first job was a house cleaner, and they did make a living for themselves, and they had success," Gordillo told Fox News in July.

The elder Gordillo's obituary portrays him as a loving and active father, noting that he raised his "children in Lakewood, Ohio" and that "his most cherished role was as a husband, father, grandfather, and uncle/tio."

"Gustavo and his parents were born in Peru and immigrated to the US," a New York City Democratic Socialists of America spokesperson told Fox News Digital following publication. "Gustavo's father grew up in Peru, not in the United States, and the family had limited contact with Gustavo's grandfather, who is the subject of the Post's recent reporting."

The New York City Democratic Socialists of America later told Fox News Digital that their co-chair's father was a product of Gordillo's first marriage.

The questions surrounding Gordillo's account of his family history come after discrepancies emerged over how he has described his occupation and living arrangements.

Democratic Socialist Headed For $142K Legislature Salary Begs For Rent Handout, Deletes Post After Backlash

The 38-year-old socialist, for example, told the New York Times that he was renting a modest apartment in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn only for it to be revealed that he was actually living in a $1.4 million townhouse owned by his father in a trendier part of the borough.

"Not only did DSA co-chair Gustavo Gordillo's parents buy him this rowhouse, they converted it from a two family and renovated it into a luxury single-family home for him," New York City Councilwoman Vickie Paladino said on X. "Exactly the kind of 'greed' the DSA rails against on a daily basis, and reducing valuable housing inventory by one more unit, which is supposedly something the DSA cares very deeply about."

Frustrated Blue-collar Union Bosses Rip Socialist Politicians, Warn Of Labor Exodus From Dem Party

Also undercutting Gordillo's working-class image is his continued self-identification as a "union electrician" despite the fact that he hasn't been a member of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers since March, when he was fired for not showing up to his apprenticeship.

"After learning of Mr. Gordillo's prolonged absence from and failure to participate in required work and classes, the trustees of the Joint Apprentice Training Committee terminated Mr. Gordillo from the program," the IBEW said in a statement.

Even with the IBEW publicly stating that Gordillo is not a member of their organization, the socialist leader still identifies himself as a "union electrician" on social media.

title: Days after Trump announces Venezuela oil deal, White House fills in some of the details
description: The White House on Monday said it’s partnering with North American Blue Energy Partners as part of President Donald Trump ’s push to tap into Venezuela’s oil industry, setting up a deal that will give...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House on Monday said it's partnering with North American Blue Energy Partners as part of President Donald Trump 's push to tap into Venezuela's oil industry, setting up a deal that will give the Pentagon a stake over roughly a fifth of the country's vast oil reserves.

The Trump administration released more details on Monday night, days after Trump announced what he described as the biggest oil deal in history. The sweeping agreement has been met with skepticism from analysts who say it will take years to revive Venezuela's production, but Trump and his aides are pitching it as a chance to develop a new oil giant in the Western Hemisphere.

As part of the deal, the U.S. is creating a private company as a joint venture with NABEP — a detail the White House had withheld for days. NABEP, owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, is already the second largest operator in Venezuela, behind Chevron.

Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodríguez is giving the company 100-year rights over 17 oil fields with proven reserves of 65 billion barrels. Many of those fields were previously owned by Russian or Chinese firms, the White House said.

In a statement Monday, Betancourt said Venezuela is "blessed with an abundance of natural resources, hardworking people and untapped potential," adding that the deal will "unleash that potential to the great benefit of both Venezuelans and Americans."

The company said Betancourt had been involved in the Venezuelan oil industry for more than 15 years and said the company has more than 5,000 employees and more than 10,000 contractors.

The deal will give the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital a 35% ownership stake in the company, the White House disclosed Monday. The U.S. will also be guaranteed a right to purchase 20% of the output at cost, orchestrated through the State Department.

The agreement was signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Betancourt's company has agreed to put up $100 billion in new oil infrastructure investments.

Trump has been pushing to boost oil production in Venezuela since the January military mission that captured then-President Nicolás Maduro on federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges.

The White House claimed the deal would be "at zero cost" to the U.S., and said the government would have veto power on board members — the majority of whom would be U.S. citizens.

"NABEP will have reputable U.S. auditors, lawyers, and advisers and the U.S. government's agreement with NABEP is governed by U.S. law and is subject to the jurisdiction of U.S. courts," the White House said in a fact sheet about the deal.

Former U.S. government energy advisers have cautioned that the deal comes with political risk, since future administrations in Venezuela or the United States could challenge the deal. Even if the agreement holds, analysts say it could take years to turn around Venezuela's dilapidated energy sector.

Trump, who says the plan will reduce gas prices, acknowledged Monday that Americans won't see change right away. Asked about a timeline at the White House, Trump said "it could be a little bit" for prices to fall, and he played down analyst predictions that it could take years.

"If it was two years, you know, that's a short period of time," he said.

Trump said the deal will provide a source to help refill America's strategic oil reserves, which have been drawn down as the Iran war chokes global oil shipments. He added that Venezuela's heavy oil will also go toward producing asphalt and other goods.

"It was this unbelievable value that was sitting dormant," Trump said of Venezuelan oil. "But we're going to be taking all of that."

Rodríguez has also spoken in favor of the deal, describing it as a chance to modernize the Venezuela's oil industry and accelerate its revival. Facing criticism that the deal cedes Venezuelan resources to the U.S., Rodríguez insisted her country's sovereignty remains secure.

Lawmakers on Capitol Hill said Monday that they were looking 

Rep. Rick Crawford, the Republican chairman of the House Intelligence Committee, said he wanted to hear details from the Trump administration "hopefully sooner rather than later."

Sen. Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said a deal that uses the military to boost a private oil venture should be rejected and said he wanted a full accounting of the legal authority for the agreement.

"President Trump's effort to turn the U.S. military into an investor in Venezuelan oil is a blatant abuse of power and taxpayer dollars," Reed said in a statement.

The new details were released a day before Trump plans to meet with a group of large and small oil refiners to discuss ways to increase America's capacity to refine oil into gasoline.

The meeting occurs as the Iran war has driven prices at the pump to a national average of $4.08, a 28% increase over the past year, according to AAA.

The White House has said that increasing the number of refineries and expanding the capacity at existing facilities would eventually reduce prices for consumers. The administration also sees the need for more refineries to process oil from Venezuela.

Also attending the meeting will be Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Jarrod Agen, the director of the White House National Energy Dominance Council.

AP Congressional Correspondent Lisa Mascaro contributed to this report.

title: Ms Rachel confronted on accusing Israel of 'genocide' in park interaction with podcaster
description: Podcaster Avi Lichtschein described confronting YouTuber Ms. Rachel at a park, where he asked her about her past comments criticizing Israel for "genocide."
fullText:
Podcaster Avi Lichtschein confronted popular children's educator Ms. Rachel about her anti-Israel comments during an interaction at a neighborhood park, according to the Sunday episode of his show, "Depends on the Context."

During the episode, Lichtschein described running into the YouTuber, whose real name is Rachel Griffin Accurso, while they were both taking their children to the park. After meeting her, he asked her why she was anti-Israel. Accurso reportedly told him that she was not anti-Israel, but anti-Israeli government and anti-Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"I pushed back on this, and I said, 'That's absurd,'" Lichtschein said. "Saying you're anti-Netanyahu, but you're not anti-Israel? Netanyahu is the democratically elected leader of the sovereign nation. I think what [she does] is way beyond that."

Youtube Star Ms Rachel Gives Funds To Democratic Socialist Michigan Senate Hopeful Abdul El-sayed

Lichtschein said that Accurso also accused Israel of committing a "genocide" through its war with Hamas.

"She said something along the lines of, 'Twenty thousand children have died. How is that not a genocide?'" Lichtschein said. "The answer is — and this is what I was trying to convey to her — genocide is not just a word for, like, a war. War is terrible. Again, Hamas started this war. Genocide is the specific accusation that [she's] hurling at the Jewish people, hurling at the state of Israel, and now it gives carte blanche to go open season on Jews literally around the world."

Lichtschein added that Accurso repeatedly said that her "husband's father is Jewish" and that she supports the existence of a Jewish state. He informed her that she was "spreading blood libel" and that there was "blood on your hands" for her ignorance before she ultimately walked away.

Scholar Challenges Ms Rachel's Gaza Messaging As Antisemitism Surges Globally

Lichtschein then spoke to Accurso's husband on the matter, apologizing for upsetting her, though he did not take back his comments.

"I wasn't planning on changing her mind," Lichstein said. "I wanted to point out your words are creating a lot of damage and someone with an audience as enormous as hers has a responsibility to understand what happens downstream from the things that she says. I think that what she's doing is motivated by compassion for children, but I think she's very naïve and gullible and doesn't realize what her actions are doing to the Jewish community at large, what her words are doing to the enemy of the Jewish people. What she's doing is harmful."

Fox News Digital reached out to Accurso for comment.

Youtube Star Ms Rachel Emotionally Apologizes For Liking Antisemitic Comment, Says It Was An Accident

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Lichtschein recalled that Accurso told him that she considers herself a "Zionist" akin to former New York City Comptroller Brad Lander.

"The timing struck me because it was such a vivid example of the point I had been trying to make to Rachel. You may personally consider yourself a Zionist and may not intend your rhetoric to contribute to hostility toward Jews or Zionists, but when you have an enormous platform, you have to think seriously about what happens downstream from the rhetoric you amplify," Lichtschein said.

He added, "I don't think Rachel hates Jews, and I'm sure her advocacy comes from a place of genuine compassion for children. But when you have an audience as enormous as hers, you have a responsibility to understand the consequences of the claims you're amplifying. That's what I wanted her to hear."
